title: Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset
description: The Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset provides estimates of annual sediment volume and reservoir sedimentation rate (RSR) for 34,372 reservoirs worldwide. The dataset was developed using the Integrated Reservoir Sedimentation Prediction (IRSP) framework, which integrates machine learning with climatic, geomorphic, hydrological, and reservoir-specific predictors. For each reservoir, the dataset provides the predicted annual sediment volume, its prediction variability quantified by the standard deviation (SD) across spatial cross-validation folds, and the RSR, defined as the ratio of annual sediment volume to initial reservoir storage capacity. Each reservoir is linked to the Global Dam Watch (GDW) v1.0 dataset through its corresponding GDW identifier.

title: Dataset and Analysis Code Supporting "Asymmetric Impacts of Supply- and Demand-Driven Flash Droughts on Leaf Senescence"
description: README This repository contains the processed datasets and R scripts supporting the manuscript entitled “Asymmetric impacts of supply- and demand-driven flash droughts on leaf senescence.” The study investigates the asymmetric effects of supply-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with precipitation deficits, and demand-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with enhanced atmospheric evaporative demand, on vegetation leaf senescence across the Northern Hemisphere during 2001–2024. The repository contains the processed datasets supporting the analyses and visualizations. Owing to repository file-size constraints, some processed datasets are provided as ZIP archives. Compression does not alter the data content, and the files should be extracted before use. Phenology_North_poly.csv contains annual satellite-derived vegetation phenological metrics for each grid cell across the Northern Hemisphere and was used for phenological quality control and anomaly calculation. all_GS_FD_years.csv contains the grid-year combinations with at least one FD overlapping the growing season and was used to identify non-FD years for calculating the phenological baseline. dEOS_poly.csv contains the resulting LSD anomalies derived from the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF). The term “EOS” used in the file name and scripts denotes the end-of-season phenological metric and corresponds to the leaf senescence date (LSD) used in the manuscript. phenology_poly_pentad.csv records the long-term mean timing of the start, peak, and end of the growing season, expressed as the corresponding 8-day periods for each grid cell. SMrz_drought_events.csv contains the flash drought events identified from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles using 01_FD_detection.R, including the original P1–P4 event timing indices, minimum soil-moisture percentile, onset rate, and cumulative severity. SMrz_drought_events_mean_environment_anomaly.csv contains flash drought events overlapping the growing season and their mean environmental anomalies calculated over the complete, untruncated P1–P4 event periods. These variables were used to characterize the hydroclimatic conditions of the events and as inputs for their subsequent classification into supply- and demand-driven flash droughts. final_FD_events.csv is the final analytical dataset and contains 1,141,551 event records. It retains the original, untruncated P1–P4 indices and was constructed by (1) retaining FD events that overlapped the growing season, (2) retaining phenological observations within the grid-specific median ± 2.5 median absolute deviations and grid cells with an interannual LSD standard deviation below 30 days, (3) retaining only grid-year combinations with a single FD overlapping the growing season, and (4) excluding non-target land-cover and biome classes, including croplands, and records with predictor values outside their respective 1st–99th percentile ranges. This dataset was used in the subsequent LSD-response, structural equation modeling, random forest, SHAP, and model-improvement analyses. Meanenv_EarlyGS_anomaly.csv and Meanenv_LateGS_anomaly.csv contain environmental anomalies during the early and late growing seasons, respectively, while Additional_data.csv provides the additional background and vegetation variables used to construct the predictor set for the RF, SHAP, and related analyses. The background spatial datasets include MODIS_IGBP0.1deg_type.csv, which contains MODIS International Geosphere–Biosphere Programme (IGBP) land-cover classifications at a spatial resolution of 0.1°; phe_poly_biome.csv, which contains biome classifications based on the World Wildlife Fund terrestrial ecoregions; and Background_MAP.csv and Background_MAT.csv, which contain mean annual precipitation and mean annual temperature, respectively. worldmap.zip contains the world map and national boundary files used for spatial visualization. The datasets supporting the response and modeling analyses include dEOSsig_supply_poly.csv and dEOSsig_demand_poly.csv, which contain the statistical significance of LSD responses to supply- and demand-driven flash droughts, respectively. RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_EVI.csv and RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_SIF.csv contain the random forest model outputs used to evaluate and compare the simulated LSD responses based on EVI and SIF. FD_ET_series.csv contains the time series of evapotranspiration anomalies before and after flash drought onset. The SHAP outputs from the random forest models are provided in shap_mat_EVI_demand.rds, shap_mat_SIF_demand.rds, shap_mat_EVI_supply.rds, and shap_mat_SIF_supply.rds. These files contain the SHAP values used to quantify and visualize the contributions of climatic, biological, and flash-drought-related variables to the modeled LSD responses under the two flash drought types. The accompanying R scripts perform the principal data processing, statistical analyses, and visualization procedures used in the study. 01_FD_detection.R identifies flash drought events from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles, calculates their characteristics, and applies the prescribed duration criterion of 4–12 consecutive 8-day periods. 02_phenology_extraction.R extracts vegetation phenological metrics from satellite-derived EVI and SIF time series. 03_FD_environment_anomaly.R retains FD events that overlap the growing season without modifying their original P1–P4 indices and calculates environmental anomalies over their complete event periods. 04_phenology_anomaly_nonFD_baseline.R calculates phenological anomalies relative to years without growing-season FDs and applies the grid-specific phenological quality-control and single-event grid-year criteria. 05_final_FD_event_filtering.R generates the final analytical dataset from the records processed in the preceding steps and applies the land-cover, biome, and predictor percentile filters. 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R conducts random forest modeling and SHAP analysis to identify the climatic and biotic controls of leaf senescence responses. 07_SEM_analysis.R performs structural equation modeling to examine the pathways through which the two flash drought types regulate leaf senescence. 08_phenology_response_significance.R evaluates the significance of phenological responses to flash droughts. 09_visualization_analysis.R generates the principal figures and statistical visualizations, and 10_visualization_SHAP_analysis.R produces the SHAP importance and dependence plots. The original satellite, reanalysis, and ancillary datasets are not redistributed in this repository, except for the processed background and boundary data used for visualization. The original root-zone soil-moisture percentile series and processed LAI time series are not redistributed because of their large file sizes; their data sources and processing procedures are documented in the manuscript and accompanying code. The original datasets are publicly available from their respective data providers, as documented in the associated manuscript. The deposited processed datasets and scripts provide the materials needed to evaluate the reported results and reproduce the principal analyses and visualizations. Code execution and software environment All scripts were developed and tested using R version 4.5.2 in RStudio under Windows. No GPU or other non-standard hardware is required for most analyses. Before running the scripts, users should replace the placeholder input, output, and figure paths at the beginning of each script with valid local paths. The scripts can then be executed directly in RStudio. The scripts are numbered according to their recommended execution order. Scripts 01_FD_detection.R–05_final_FD_event_filtering.R perform FD detection, phenological extraction, anomaly calculation, and construction of the final analytical dataset. Scripts 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R–08_phenology_response_significance.R perform the RF–SHAP, SEM, and significance analyses, respectively. The final visualization scripts generate the figures reported in the manuscript. The deposited processed datasets allow the principal statistical analyses and figures to be reproduced without rerunning the complete processing chain from the original satellite and reanalysis data. Using the prepared input datasets, all scripts except 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R typically complete within several minutes, although runtime depends on computer performance and data-transfer speed. The complete random forest and SHAP workflow in 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R was run on a multicore server and required approximately four days. This script calculates one response–FD-type SHAP combination per run and should be executed for the four combinations of EVI/SIF and supply-/demand-driven FDs to regenerate all deposited SHAP objects. The principal R packages and tested versions were: data.table 1.17.8, dplyr 1.1.4, zoo 1.8-12, doSNOW 1.0.20, foreach 1.5.2, ranger 0.17.0, ggplot2 4.0.0, patchwork 1.3.2, RColorBrewer 1.1-3, usdm 2.1-7, ALEPlot 1.1, mlbench 2.1-6, fastshap 0.1.1, future 1.33.2, lavaan 0.6-17, raster 3.6-26, terra 1.7-78, sf 1.0-23, plyr 1.8.9, and scales 1.4.0. A complete README file and R session record will be included with the code archive in the next repository version.

title: Dataset for "Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan, Atmos. Environ."
description: This dataset is for “Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan” by Wei et al. in Atmospheric Environment. The contents are described in the sheet “Readme” of the Excel file named “Dataset_cw260904.xlsx”. The dataset contains the data used in the manuscript, including average fluorescence spectra, fluorescence indices, atmospheric fluorescence volumes, normalized fluorescence volumes, and PARAFAC components of water-soluble organic matter (WSOM) in atmospheric aerosol samples collected at forest, remote, and urban sites in Japan. The dataset also includes the correlations of the atmospheric fluorescence volumes of the PARAFAC components with the concentrations of water-soluble organic carbon (WSOC) and meteorological parameters. The dataset further provides fluorescence indices and atmospheric fluorescence volumes for three subfractions of WSOM obtained from aerosol and rainwater samples collected in Nagoya. The excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectra of WSOM in aqueous extracts were measured using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (FP-6600, JASCO) with a 1-cm path length quartz cell. The ranges of the excitation and emission wavelengths were 235-500 nm and 300-600 nm, respectively. The drEEM toolbox for MATLAB was used to preprocess the EEMs and to perform parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis. The concentrations of WSOC and water-soluble inorganic ions were measured using a total organic carbon analyzer and ion chromatography, respectively. The dataset was obtained in the study conducted under JSPS KAKENHI (JP26281007, JP23H00515, and JP19KK0265); ArCS II (JPMXD1420318865); and ERDF from ERCA (JPMEERF20232001). Other acknowledgments are provided in the associated manuscript.

title: Analysis-derived datasets for: "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins"
description: Derived datasets underlying Ismail and Yamashiki, "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins", submitted to Earth Systems and Environment. The study assesses fluvial flood hazard and population exposure across Pakistan's five major drainage basins (872,782 km², 99% of national territory) from the 50-year to the 500-year return period, combining Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) inundation mapping with GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge, Generalised Extreme Value flood frequency analysis, and hydraulic-geometry depth estimation. A first-order sensitivity decomposition attributes total exposure uncertainty to four sources: rating curve parameters, DEM resolution, GEV parameter uncertainty and population data uncertainty. CONTENTS Derived datasets (14 CSV files) AMS_5basins.csv annual maximum series, five basins, 1979-2025 GEV_parameters_47yr.csv fitted GEV location, scale and shape parameters gev_shape_intervals.csv 95% intervals on the shape parameter GEV_return_levels_47yr.csv return levels, T50 to T500 prep_design_discharges.csv design discharges by basin and return period prep_depths.csv design depths from the generalised rating curve prep_depth_agreement.csv depth agreement across rating curve formulations prep_exposure_90m.csv population and built-up exposure, 90 m framework prep_exposure_southern_30m.csv Southern Basin exposure at 30 m prep_exposure_ranges.csv exposure ranges and range factors by basin prep_national_totals.csv national exposure totals prep_uncertainty_decomposition.csv four-source sensitivity decomposition prep_central_bayes.csv Central Basin Bayesian GEV estimates prior_sensitivity_grid.csv prior sensitivity for the Bayesian fit Published tables (22 CSV files) Every table in the paper as a separate file: the five main tables (Table1-Table5) and all seventeen supplementary table parts (TableS1-TableS14, including the a/b splits of S5, S6 and S12), exactly as published. Every number reported in the paper can be checked directly against these files. NOT INCLUDED Input rasters and gauge records are third-party data distributed under their own terms and are not redistributed here. Their sources and versions are listed in the paper's Data Availability statement: GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge v4.0 (Copernicus Climate Change Service); SRTM 30 m and 90 m (NASA Earthdata, USGS EarthExplorer); GHS-POP and GHS-BUILT-S R2023A epoch 2025 (European Commission JRC); HydroBASINS Level 4 (HydroSHEDS); Sentinel-1 GRD (Copernicus, via Google Earth Engine); Global Flood Database 2010 extent. Gauge records are available from the Global Runoff Data Centre, Koblenz, on request under their data-sharing policy and are not redistributable. Analysis code is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. CHANGES FROM VERSION 1.0 Version 1.0 (April 2026) accompanied the originally submitted manuscript. This version corresponds to the revised manuscript and supersedes it. The sensitivity decomposition has been recomputed: the population uncertainty term now uses the full width of the symmetric ±30% bound on gridded population counts, as set out in Section 3.7 of the revised paper. Shape-parameter confidence intervals, design depths, Southern Basin dual-resolution exposure and the full set of published tables have been added.

title: ERA5–SARAH-3 Meteorological Cutouts for Renewable Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
description: Description This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling. The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline. All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes. Data Sources ERA5 ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are: height: Surface elevation wnd100m: Wind speed at 100 m above ground level wnd_azimuth: Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field roughness: Surface roughness length influx_toa: Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation albedo: Surface albedo temperature: Air temperature at 2 m above ground level soil temperature: Soil temperature at level 4 runoff: Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ SARAH-3 Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3: influx_direct: Direct surface solar radiation influx_diffuse: Diffuse surface solar radiation The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing: solar_altitude: Solar altitude angle solar_azimuth: Solar azimuth angle Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN. title: Soil Organic Carbon Threshold and Historical-baseline Datasets Underlying a Soil Degradation Boundary Assessment for India
description: Overview This record contains the full dataset (data/) supporting the Research Paper titled Integrating functionally-based soil organic carbon threshold models with reconstructed historical baselines to evaluate a soil degradation boundary in India and every raw/reconstructed geospatial input, every pixel- and ecoregion-level analysis-ready table, and every precomputed intermediate result (threshold-fit curves, sensitivity and resilience classifications) used to generate the Research paper results using the code accessible openly as Jupyter-notebook analysis code on https://github.com/sirtiza34/SOC_Functional_Thresholds_India_Analysis and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22806576. Together they allow full reproduction of the Research Paper's quantitative results. All the dataset files are distributed only through this Zenodo record and the code repositories document this and points here. Spatial and temporal scope The dataset covers the soilscapes delimited by the territorial extents of India. Contemporary layers are at 250 m pixel resolution (50.48 million pixels) and temporal snapshot of 2019 developed from the SOC concentration data available at https://soilgrids.org/. The historical baseline is sourced from the Sanderman et al. (2017)’s paleo-SOC reconstructions available at https://github.com/whrc/Soil-Carbon-Debt. The baseline is reconstructed on a coarser (~10 km) grid. All analyses are synthesized to 49 terrestrial ecoregions (World Wildlife Federation) covering the territory of India, and further stratified into 1,156 ecoregion × soil-order × land-use Environmental Context Units (ECUs) for threshold assignment. Contents, by category Pixel-level analysis-ready tables (the three large files) master_analysis_database.parquet — the master contemporary pixel database, 50.48 million rows, carrying assigned functional thresholds and derived metrics for every 250 m pixel in India. step6_functional_state_sample.csv — a spatially block-declustered sample of 395,750 pixels carrying per-pixel probability of being below threshold, P(SOC<T), for each of the four response domains. step4_distance_sample.csv — a pixel sample used to compute distance-to-functional-transition. Geospatial layers (rasters and vectors) ecoregion_id.tif, accel_class_map.tif, step10_feature_stack.tif, step13_soc_stack.tif — raster layers used in mapping and feature construction. step11_map_c_class_raster.npy / step14_boundary_raster.npy (with matching *_meta.pkl files) — precomputed classification and boundary-classification rasters plus their georeferencing metadata. india_boundary.geojson — national boundary vector used for map masking/plotting. Ecoregion-level and threshold tables About 30 CSV files cover, among others, the common analytical framework and state variables per ecoregion, tiered threshold assignment and tier-usage area shares, national and per-ecoregion threshold estimates and their uncertainty, historical-depletion/functional-risk correlation by response domain, degradation-boundary classification per ecoregion, area-weighted vs. unit-weighted synthesis, directional consistency and cross-domain overlap, resilience-opportunity and continued-loss-risk groupings, degradation hotspot lists, and area-weighting tables. Precomputed model curves step12_curves.pkl, step13_curves.pkl — fitted threshold-response curve objects. Data provenance Historical SOC baseline: depth-integrated (0–30 cm) reconstruction following the global SOC-debt method of Sanderman, Hengl & Fiske (2017, PNAS). Contemporary soil properties: SoilGrids v2.0 (Poggio et al., 2021, SOIL). Ecoregion boundaries: WWF terrestrial ecoregions. File formats GeoTIFF (.tif), NumPy array (.npy) with pickled metadata (.pkl), GeoJSON (.geojson), Apache Parquet (.parquet), and CSV — all openly readable with standard open-source GIS/Python tooling (rasterio, pyarrow, pandas, geopandas).

title: Global 0.05° 8-day Gridded TROPOMI Solar-Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence (dcSIF) from ANN-based Retrievals, May 2018 – July 2025
description: This dataset provides global gridded solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) derived from TROPOMI (Sentinel-5P) observations at 0.05° spatial resolution and 8-day temporal resolution, covering the period from 1 May 2018 to 31 July 2025. The input data are ungridded (Level-2) SIF soundings retrieved using the artificial neural network (ANN) approach developed by Li et al.(10.1016/j.rse.2025.114987), which are publicly available on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/16537343). These soundings were aggregated onto a regular grid following the oversampling approach of Frankenberg et al., as implemented in SatelliteGridding.jl (https://github.com/cfranken/SatelliteGridding). The variable dcSIF denotes daily-corrected SIF, obtained by applying the day-length correction factor following Köhler et al.(https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GL079031), which scales instantaneous SIF to daily average values. Data are provided as one NetCDF file per year. Citation: If you use this dataset, please cite the original SIF retrieval paper by Li et al. (2025; 10.1016/j.rse.2025.114987), as well as the methodological references listed above where appropriate.

title: A Global Soil Spectral Library and Soil Organic Carbon Estimation Dataset Based on Geographical Stratification
description: This dataset comprises 784 topsoil samples selected from the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), including soil organic carbon content, geographic coordinates, and visible–near-infrared spectral data covering 400–2400 nm at a standardized 10 nm interval. The dataset also integrates ten environmental covariates: clay content, silt content, cation exchange capacity, soil pH, elevation, slope, annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, NDVI, and land-cover type. Based on these covariates, the samples were classified into five geographical environmental zones using a Gaussian mixture model. The dataset supports comparisons between global and geographically stratified models for soil organic carbon estimation and facilitates the regional application of global soil spectral libraries.

title: EcoTwin Model Input Data Collection in Uniform Format
description: Lake-Specific ERA5, ISIMIP3b and ESA CCI Lakes Datasets Overview: This repository contains lake-specific climate and lake-observation datasets extracted and processed from three established data products: - ERA5 meteorological data - ISIMIP3b climate forcing data - ESA CCI Lakes Level-3S merged products, version 2.1 The datasets were extracted for four study lakes: - Lake Balaton - Lake Iseo - Lake Mälaren - Lake Wylerbergmeer The processing workflow identifies the source-data grid cells intersecting each lake, extracts the corresponding time series, and produces lake-specific NetCDF datasets suitable for subsequent analysis. **Important:** The files in this repository are derived/extracted products. They do not replace the original ERA5, ISIMIP3b, or ESA CCI Lakes datasets. Users should consult and cite the original data providers and comply with the terms and licences of the original datasets. Study lakes: | Lake | ERA5 grid cells | ISIMIP3b grid cells | ESA CCI Lakes | | Balaton | 7 | 4 | Available (ID 310) | | Iseo | 1 | 2 | Available (ID 300014185) | | Mälaren | 17 | 9 | Available (ID 163) | | Wylerbergmeer | 1 | 1 | Not available | The lake polygons for Balaton, Iseo and Mälaren were obtained from HydroLAKES. A custom shapefile was used for Wylerbergmeer. 1. ERA5 meteorological data 1.1 Grid-cell identification The ERA5 workflow identifies the ERA5 0.25° × 0.25° grid cells that intersect each study lake. For each lake: - The lake polygon is read from HydroLAKES or the custom Wylerbergmeer shapefile. - The lake bounding box is calculated. - A regular 0.25° latitude–longitude ERA5 grid is generated over the bounding box. - Square polygons representing the ERA5 grid cells are created around each grid-cell centre. - Spatial intersection is used to identify all grid cells intersecting the lake polygon. - The coordinates of the selected grid-cell centres are extracted. 1.2 ERA5 data extraction Hourly ERA5 single-level meteorological data are downloaded for each selected grid cell using the Copernicus Climate Data Store and the ecmwfr R package. The extraction period is: 1980-01-01 to 2026-05-31 The following variables are included: | Variable | ERA5 short name | Units | | 2 m air temperature | t2m | K | | 2 m dew point temperature | d2m | K | | Surface pressure | sp | Pa | | Surface solar radiation downwards | ssrd | J m⁻² | | Surface thermal radiation downwards | strd | J m⁻² | | Total precipitation | tp | m | | 10 m zonal wind component | u10 | m s⁻¹ | | 10 m meridional wind component | v10 | m s⁻¹ | | Total cloud cover | tcc | fraction (0–1) | 1.3 ERA5 merging The individual ERA5 grid-cell NetCDF files are merged into one multi-station NetCDF file per lake. The merged datasets contain: - A common time dimension (valid_time) - Station identifiers corresponding to ERA5 grid cells - Latitude and longitude for each grid cell - Meteorological variables stored as time × station arrays; - Selected metadata copied from the original ERA5 files, including units, long names and standard names. Final files: - lake_balaton_era5.nc - lake_iseo_era5.nc - lake_mälaren_era5.nc - lake_wylerbergmeer_era5.nc 2. ESA CCI Lakes products 2.1 Data source and extraction Daily ESA CCI Lakes Level-3S merged products, version 2.1, are downloaded from the CEDA THREDDS server for 1992–2022. A unique ESA CCI Lakes ID is used to isolate each lake from the static lake mask. | Lake | ESA CCI Lakes ID | | Mälaren | 163 | | Balaton | 310 | | Iseo | 300014185 | | Wylerbergmeer | Not available | Wylerbergmeer is therefore excluded from the ESA CCI Lakes dataset. 2.2 Spatial processing The static CCI_lakeid mask is used to: - Identify all grid cells belonging to the selected lake ID - Calculate a bounding box around the selected pixels, with a one-pixel buffer - Extract a reduced spatial subset from the global dataset After subsetting, all variables are masked so that only pixels belonging to the selected lake ID remain valid. Other pixels are assigned _FillValue. 2.3 Variables The extracted ESA CCI Lakes variables are: | Variable | Name | Units | | Lake surface water temperature | lake_surface_water_temperature | K | | LSWT uncertainty | lswt_uncertainty | K | | Chlorophyll-a concentration | chla_mean | mg m⁻³ | | Chlorophyll-a uncertainty | chla_uncertainty | % | | Turbidity | turbidity_mean | NTU | | Turbidity uncertainty | turbidity_uncertainty | % | | Lake ice cover class | lake_ice_cover_class | categorical | | Lake surface water extent | lake_surface_water_extent | km² | | Water surface height above reference datum | water_surface_height_above_reference_datum | m | Associated quality-control variables include: lswt_quality_level, lwlr_quality_flag, lwe_quality_flag and lwl_quality_flag. 2.4 Quality control LSWT LSWT and its uncertainty are retained only for: lswt_quality_level = 4 or 5 Values equal to the specified fill value are removed, and invalid pixels are set to NA. Chlorophyll-a chla_mean and chla_uncertainty are filtered using lwlr_quality_flag. Pixels for which the relevant poor/low-consistency quality bits are set are removed. Turbidity Turbidity and its uncertainty use the same lwlr_quality_flag filtering approach as chlorophyll-a. Ice cover Only the following classes are retained: 1 = water and 2 = ice. All other values are assigned NA. Lake surface water extent Only lwe_quality_flag = 0 (good) and lwe_quality_flag = 1 (medium) are retained. Water level Only lwl_quality_flag = 0 (good) and lwl_quality_flag = 1 (medium) are retained. 2.5 Final CCI Lakes datasets After filtering, daily files are merged along a new time dimension. The final NetCDF datasets have dimensions: lat × lon × time Final files: - lake_mälaren_cci_lakes.nc - lake_balaton_cci_lakes.nc - lake_iseo_cci_lakes.nc 3. ISIMIP3b climate data 3.1 Grid-cell identification The ISIMIP3b workflow identifies the 0.5° × 0.5° grid cells intersecting each study lake. For each lake: - The lake polygon is read from HydroLAKES or the custom Wylerbergmeer shapefile. - A regular 0.5° latitude–longitude grid is generated. - Grid-cell polygons are created around each grid-cell centre. - Spatial intersection identifies the grid cells intersecting the lake. - The selected grid-cell centre coordinates are stored. 3.2 Climate models The ISIMIP3b data include the following GCMs: - GFDL-ESM4 - IPSL-CM6A-LR - MPI-ESM1-2-HR - MRI-ESM2-0 - UKESM1-0-LL 3.3 Scenarios The following scenarios are included: | Simulation | Period | | Historical | 1850–2014 | | SSP126 | 2015–2100 | | SSP370 | 2015–2100 | | SSP585 | 2015–2100 | 3.4 Variables | Variable | ISIMIP3b short name | Units | | Near-surface air temperature | tas | K | | Daily maximum air temperature | tasmax | K | | Daily minimum air temperature | tasmin | K | | Near-surface relative humidity | hurs | % | | Near-surface specific humidity | huss | kg kg⁻¹ | | Surface air pressure | ps | Pa | | Precipitation | pr | kg m⁻² s⁻¹ | | Surface downwelling shortwave radiation | rsds | W m⁻² | | Surface downwelling longwave radiation | `rlds` | W m⁻² | | Near-surface wind speed | sfcWind | m s⁻¹ | 3.5 Extraction and merging The global ISIMIP3b NetCDF files are opened and the grid cells identified for each lake are extracted. The extracted 10-year chunks are concatenated to reconstruct continuous time series for: - historical: 1850–2014 - SSP126: 2015–2100 - SSP370: 2015–2100 - SSP585: 2015–2100 The time axis is reconstructed using the same time origin across the complete period. Latitude and longitude are retained for each grid cell, and variables are assembled into time × station arrays. Selected metadata, including units, long names, standard names and selected global attributes, are copied from the original ISIMIP3b files. The final output is one multi-station NetCDF file per lake, GCM and scenario. title: The Global Carbon Budget (GCB) Allocation Debate in Post-Paris Climate Politics: New Insights for Current Discussions-Database Construction
description: The deposit contains three tables. gcb_panel.csv is a country–year panel with 13,327 rows covering 1990–2050: greenhouse gas emissions in CO₂e with and without LULUCF, population observed to 2019 and projected thereafter, and GDP at current and at constant 2015 prices. gcb_indicators.csv holds one row per country with every allocation indicator, the components of the re-specified ECPC, and the descriptive weights. gcb_national_budgets.csv converts each share into an allocation in GtCO₂e, into years of 2019 emissions, and into the constant annual reduction rate that exhausts it by 2050, for every combination of criterion and budget scenario. codebook.md defines every variable with its unit, time window and source, and is regenerated from the configuration file on every run, so it cannot drift from the calculation. MANIFEST.json records the SHA-256 checksum of each of the 12 source files and of each output, together with the versions of Python and of every library used. A single command, run_all.py, rebuilds everything from the frozen sources and exits with a non-zero status if the replication of the published tables fails.

title: Code and trained model weights for "GRBD: A Global-Scale Multiple-Type River Barrier Annotation Database for Global River Barrier Mapping with Deep Learning"
description: This Zenodo record contains code and analysis data supporting a study on deep-learning-based mapping and evaluation of river barriers. The materials cover annotation-format conversion, dataset preparation, model training and inference, detection-performance evaluation, approximate barrier-size classification, and cross-basin barrier-density analysis. The repository includes scripts for converting LabelMe annotations to YOLO and COCO formats, randomly splitting a COCO dataset into training, validation, and test subsets using an 8:1:1 ratio, training YOLO11 and RT-DETRv2 models, conducting batch inference with RT-DETRv2, and evaluating predictions against manually interpreted ground-truth annotations using intersection over union (IoU). An additional script estimates approximate barrier lengths from annotated coordinates and classifies barriers into three size classes (≤30 m, 30–100 m, and >100 m). The record also includes analysis data for 58 selected sub-basins used to compare barrier counts and densities derived from three sources: manual visual interpretation, deep-learning predictions, and Global Dam Watch (GDW). These data were used for the statistical analyses reported in the associated study. The object-detection workflow includes six river-barrier classes: weir, dam, sluice, tide, earth, and lock. Some scripts retain environment-specific file paths and therefore require users to modify input/output paths before execution. RT-DETRv2 and YOLO scripts also depend on their respective external frameworks, configuration files, and model weights. Further details are provided in the accompanying README. RT-DETRv2-x-bestpt.zip contains the trained weights of the best-performing RT-DETRv2-X model used in this study. The model was selected for subsequent cross-basin generalization testing and river-barrier detection analyses.

title: 13 October 2019 Pléiades (CNES) pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli catastrophic flood
description: Updated version of the 2 m merged Pléiades DEM where a ~10 m horizontal shift was corrected. =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal (Rasuwa) and Tibet : (see e.g. https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/) We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades tri-stereo acquired on the 13 October 2019, 7 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The updated collection includes one DEM : 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The three Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Shean et al., 2016, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total nine DEMs in 2x2m, 4x4m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean's demcoreg (https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/72886193) implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). Then, for each GSD (20m, 4m and 2m), the three DEMs are mosaicked using the median value. 2019-10-13_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the three above DEMs retaining the highest resolution (2 m)where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. title: GLCD250-MOD: Global Lakes Chlorophyll-a Daily 250 m based on MODIS — Part 1 of 3 (Lake IDs 1–50)
description: GLCD250-MOD is a global dataset of chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentrations for inland lakes. title: Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change
description: Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change 1. Overview This archive contains the processed data, Python scripts, reproduced figure outputs, and per-figure statistics used for the manuscript "Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change". The original daily meteorological forcing data and high-resolution process-based model outputs for 1,427,688 lakes are too large to include here. The archive instead provides processed lake-level, gridded, validation, and figure-source datasets sufficient to reproduce the main quantitative results and figures included in this package. 2. Getting Started and System Requirements 2.1 Zenodo Archives and Extraction The repository is distributed as standard ZIP archives and approximately 1 GB file parts so that large downloads can be transferred reliably: README.md: documentation for archive extraction, software setup, data contents, and reproduction. lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip: script/ and requirements.txt. lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip: demo data, external geospatial data, and processed data (including lake_qc_exclusions.csv) other than the two largest NPZ files. lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part007: parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/daily_nonoverlap_results.npz. lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part011: parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/background_results.npz. lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip: 26 reference PDF/JPG files for 13 manuscript figures and 13 per-figure statistics CSV files, regenerated in the latest test run. Demo outputs are generated separately by script/demo.py. The README, scripts, core data archive, and every part of both large data archives are required to rerun every analysis. The results archive is optional and provides reference outputs for comparison. Download all required files into one directory. Individual .partNNN files cannot be extracted directly; they must first be joined in numerical order. On macOS, open Terminal in the download directory and run: cat lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip cat lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip mkdir -p lake_thermal_structure cp README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure cd lake_thermal_structure On Windows 11, open PowerShell in the download directory. Paste and run the entire function definition below before running the two Join-FileParts commands. Each command reports the part being joined and the completed ZIP path. Joining several gigabytes may take a few minutes. function Join-FileParts($Pattern, $OutputFile, [int]$ExpectedParts) { $directory = (Get-Location).ProviderPath $parts = @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $directory -Filter $Pattern -File | Sort-Object Name) if ($parts.Count -ne $ExpectedParts) { throw "Expected $ExpectedParts parts in $directory; found $($parts.Count)." } for ($i = 0; $i -lt $ExpectedParts; $i++) { $expected = $OutputFile + ('.part{0:D3}' -f $i) if ($parts[$i].Name -ne $expected) { throw "Missing or incorrectly named part: $expected" } } $outputPath = Join-Path $directory $OutputFile $temporaryPath = $outputPath + '.joining' $outputStream = [System.IO.File]::Create($temporaryPath) try { foreach ($part in $parts) { Write-Host "Joining $($part.Name)..." $partStream = [System.IO.File]::OpenRead($part.FullName) try { $partStream.CopyTo($outputStream) } finally { $partStream.Dispose() } } } finally { $outputStream.Dispose() } $expectedSize = ($parts | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum).Sum if ((Get-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath).Length -ne $expectedSize) { throw "Joined file size does not match the total part size." } Move-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath -Destination $outputPath -Force Write-Host "Completed: $outputPath" } Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip" 8 Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip" 12 New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force lake_thermal_structure | Out-Null Copy-Item README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure Set-Location lake_thermal_structure The commands use built-in macOS and Windows 11 tools. If the optional results ZIP was not downloaded, omit its tar -xf command. Extracting the archives into the same destination reconstructs this layout: lake_thermal_structure/ ├── README.md ├── requirements.txt ├── script/ ├── data/ └── results/ 2.2 Hardware A standard desktop or laptop computer can run the scripts, but the full data workflow is memory intensive. We recommend: RAM: at least 64 GB for the full datasets included here. Storage: at least 25 GB for the extracted repository and generated outputs. Allow at least 65 GB of free space while joining and extracting all downloaded archive parts; the downloaded parts and reconstructed ZIP files can be deleted after successful extraction. GPU: not required. Non-standard hardware: not required. The lightweight Poyang Lake demo dataset requires substantially less memory than the full figure workflows. 2.3 Software Setup and First Run The scripts were developed and tested with Python 3.13.5 on Windows 11. Required Python packages are listed in requirements.txt. Install them and run the lightweight demo from the reconstructed repository root: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python script/demo.py The demo writes its outputs to results/demo/. Full manuscript figures can be regenerated with the commands in Section 6. Generating each figure takes approximately 10 minutes. Figure 4 may take longer time for its large amount of data input. title: Developing a dynamic semi-distributed hydrological model considering interactions between soil moisture and evapotranspiration: application of bulk transfer method
description: Empirically-derived relationships are mainly used to estimate evapotranspiration (ET) in water balance models. Due to a lack of effective factors and correct conceptual relationships, the resulting ET may be inaccurate. Therefore, a hydrological model was developed by combining water balance and bulk transfer theory, called semi-distributed coupled water balance and bulk transfer (SD-CWBT). According to it, a dynamic interrelationship between ET and soil moisture was correctly established to estimate ET via physical concepts. Global gridded ET retrievals, which provide the spatiotemporal distribution of ET at a global scale, including ECMWF Reanalysis v5-Land (ERA5-Land), TERRA, Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and Operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop), were employed to evaluate the model. The results indicated the SD-CWBT, with Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of [0.6, 0.95], [0.68, 0.96], and [12.61, 0.99] for the streamflow and groundwater level simulation, respectively, had better performance compared to the alternatives. Furthermore, the estimated spatiotemporal distributions of ET agreed well with the climatic-vegetation conditions.

title: Data and code supporting concurrent burned-area detections and persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon
description: This release supports the study “Concurrent burned-area detections are associated with persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon”. Version 1.1.0 adds Supplementary_Data_1_Active_Fire_Analysis.zip, containing the complementary historical NASA FIRMS MODIS and Suomi-NPP VIIRS analysis, the fixed protocol, input data, derived matching results, scripts, environment requirements, provenance, checksums, tests and independent verification results. Download and extract this ZIP without changing its folder structure, then open 08_VALIDACION_FUEGO_ACTIVO/START_HERE_REVIEWERS.md. The ZIP is 17,955,692 bytes and contains 59 files. The original cohort archive fire_loss_conversion_peruvian_amazon_v1.0.0.zip and its separate companion files are preserved unchanged. Those historical companions retain the original title, DOI, version and figure numbering. For this release, read START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md and use CITATION_VERSION_1_1_0.cff. The original release remains available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21881539. The study uses a retrospective spatial cohort sampled on a systematic 0.01° lattice in stable forests of the Peruvian Amazon. Hansen Global Forest Change defines first loss during 2014–2021; MapBiomas Peru Collection 3 defines baseline and subsequent land cover; MapBiomas Fire and GABAM define concurrent burned-area detection categories. Persistent conversion requires anthropogenic cover in each of three consecutive post-loss years. The original archive reproduces analyses from derived panels, not the raster-to-panel extraction. The estimates are associational. Thermal observations corroborate nearby combustion but do not validate individual 30 m burned pixels or subsequent land use. title: SCOPE / NCEO: Monthly global Marine Phytoplankton Primary Production, between 1998-2025 at 9 km resolution (derived from the Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative v6.0)
description: This dataset contains global, monthly marine phytoplankton primary production products (in mg C m-2 d-1) for the period of 1998 to 2025 at 9 km spatial resolution. Data are provided in NetCDF format. Primary production by marine phytoplankton was modelled using ocean-colour remote sensing products and a spectrally-resolved primary production model that incorporates the vertical structure of phytoplankton and simulates changes in photosynthesis as a function of irradiance using a two-parameter photosynthesis versus irradiance (P-I) function (see Kulk et al. 2020, Sathyendranath et al. 2020a, and references therein for details). Chlorophyll-a products were obtained from the European Space Agency (ESA) Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI v6 dataet). Photosynthetic Active Radiation (PAR) products were obtained from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and were corrected for inter-sensor bias in products. In situ datasets of chlorophyll-a profile parameters and P-I parameters were incorporated as described in Kulk et al. (2020). The primary production products were generated as part of the European Space Agency (ESA) project 'Satellite-based observations of Carbon in the Ocean: Pools, fluxes and Exchanges' (SCOPE). Support from the National Centre of Earth Observation (NCEO) is also acknowledged. title: Satellite-derived evaluation of thermal and non-thermal controls on seawater CO2 fugacity along the Nordic Seas during spring - Data availability
description: We present the dataset (in .csv) of sea surface temperature (SST, in °C), sea surface salinity (SSS), chlorophyll-a (Chl-a, in mg m³) and sea surface CO2 fugacity (fCO2, in µatm) used for the development of the fCO2 model. Recalculated measurements of fCO2 were extracted from cruises with quality control flags A and B in the Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas version 2025 (SOCAT v2025, https://doi.org/10.25921/648f-fv35). SST and SSS data were extracted from the L4 product Multi Observation Global Ocean ARMOR3D (https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00052) matching the in situ fCO2 measurements in a spatial resolution of 0.25°. Satellite-derived Chl-a data was extracted from daily images from the ESA Ocean Color Climate Change Initiative 6.0 database (https://www.oceancolour.org/) matching the in situ fCO2 measurements in a spatial resolution of 1 km. We also present the recalculated spatial fields (in .nc) of SST (in °C), SSS, Chl-a (in mg m³), fCO2 (in µatm) and calculated uncertainty (in µatm) for March, April and May between 2010 and 2025, with a spatial resolution of 0.125°.

title: Geospatial Dataset of Forest Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization in La Malinche, Mexico: 2019 Random Forest–Derived Canopy-Height and Structural Products and Structural Products Derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map
description: La Malinche Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization (LMCHSR) is a public geospatial dataset of forest canopy height and structural regionalization for an area of interest encompassing the La Montaña Malinche o Matlalcuéyatl Federal Protected Natural Area, Mexico, and the adjacent peripheral area included in the analysis. The 2019 canopy-height raster was produced by integrating three Random Forest models corresponding to Sentinel-2 Level-2A acquisitions on 22 January, 28 March, and 12 April 2019. Each model used the red (B4), red-edge (B5), and shortwave-infrared (B12) bands, together with elevation and slope, as predictors. Canopy heights from CHMv2 (Brandt et al., 2026) served as the response reference after spatial harmonization to the 10 m modeling grid. The date-specific predictions were integrated into a multitemporal canopy-height surface. Structural products were derived from this RF surface on a 20 m analytical grid. They include structural objects, aggregated regions, five canopy-height classes (S01–S05), and connected class patches. An independent set of 20 m structural products was derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map of Lang et al. (2023), with separately determined objects, regions, and five classes (E01–E05). The harmonized source ETH canopy-height raster is not redistributed. The release contains 18 geospatial assets: one area-of-interest boundary, the 2019 RF canopy-height raster (RF 2019), eight RF-derived structural products, and eight ETH2020-derived structural products. Raster and vector files are supplied as GeoTIFF and GeoPackage files, respectively, using the WGS 84 / UTM zone 14N coordinate reference system (CRS; EPSG:32614). The release also includes metadata, dictionaries, a class legend, and Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) checksums. The two structural classifications were generated independently; matching class codes do not imply identical class definitions or direct temporal forest change.

title: Pantropical calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) of cropland and grassland at 30 m (2020-2024)
description: This dataset provides annual calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) for cropland and grassland at 30 m spatial resolution for the pantropical belt (48°S-36°N) for the years 2020-2024, and the rate of change of GPP for both land-cover classes. The calibrated GPP is derived from the Global Pasture Watch uncalibrated GPP (uGPP) product (Isik et al., 2025), which uses a uniform light-use efficiency (LUE) of 1 gC m-2 d-1 MJ-1 across all land cover types. Here, uGPP is multiplied, pixel by pixel and year by year, by a land-cover-specific LUE factor taken from the Global Harmonized Land Cover (Moreno et al., 2026) map of the same year. The result is then masked to the cropland and grassland classes of that year. Layers Layer Value Unit Data type NoData Annual GPP (cropland) calibrated GPP of the year gC m-2 yr-1 UInt16 65535 Annual GPP (grassland) calibrated GPP of the year gC m-2 yr-1 UInt16 65535 Rate of change 2020-2024 (cropland) [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 gC m-2 yr-1 per year Float32 -9999 Rate of change 2020-2024 (grassland) [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 gC m-2 yr-1 per year Float32 -9999 Methods Input alignment. The annual uGPP and GHLC land cover maps for 2020-2024 were placed on one common grid (0.00025°, EPSG:4326) using virtual rasters (VRT). Both products share the same pixel grid, so no resampling was applied. Calibration. For every pixel and year: GPP = uGPP × LUE(land-cover class of the same year), using the LUE factors below. uGPP values ≥ 65000 and land-cover nodata (255) are treated as nodata. Values are rounded to 1 gC m-2 yr-1. Masking. The annual GPP was retained only where the land cover for that year belongs to the cropland (classes 2-9) or grassland (classes 10-11) group; all other pixels are nodata. Rate of change. Computed from the masked annual GPP as rate = [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4, i.e. the difference between the late and the early two-year means, divided by the 2020-2024 period length (4 years). A pixel has a rate only if it belongs to the group in all four years used (2020, 2021, 2023, 2024) and has valid, non-capped GPP in all of them. Processing and quality control. Processing was done in 1° × 1° tiles in parallel. Each tile is tagged with the input version and a fingerprint of the LUE table. After processing, all tiles were scanned for block-shaped gaps caused by failed data transfers (areas missing in one year but valid in all other years); affected tiles were recomputed. title: Code and data for: Ignoring plant responses to rising CO₂ overestimates dryland expansion under high emissions in a Brazilian Cerrado agricultural frontier (MATOPIBA)
description: Python pipeline and data used to compare potential evapotranspiration (PET) with and without the stomatal effect of CO₂ over MATOPIBA, Brazil (964 cells of 0.25°, about 736,000 km²). PET-PM is the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation with fixed surface resistance; PET-Y is the formulation of Yang et al. (2019), in which surface resistance increases with CO₂, driven by OCO-2 xCO₂. The record covers the observed period (2015–2025: xCO₂, PET, SIF from GOSIF, aridity index) and future scenarios (RCP 2.6, 4.5 and 8.5; 2021–2040, 2041–2060 and 2081–2100), including the CO₂ offset and the area susceptible to desertification (UNCCD classes). Contents: scripts/ (pipeline, run in numerical order), data_raw/ (raw downloads clipped to MATOPIBA: ERA5-Land daily by year, OCO-2 Lite soundings, GOSIF), data/ (processed monthly grids, MATOPIBA boundary, CMIP5 regional deltas), results/ (tables and gridded outputs used in the article) and figures/ (final figures). The file data/era5land_diario.nc is not included and is rebuilt from data_raw/ by scripts/01_download_gee.py. Code is released under the MIT licence (LICENSE); data and figures under CC BY 4.0. title: Reshuihe watershed, Liangshan (China): online household survey, fire-prevention burden and greening — data and code
description: De-identified data, analysis code and analysis outputs for a study of ecological restoration ("greening"), wildfire and fire-prevention duties in the Reshuihe watershed (174.7 km²), Xide County, Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan, China. Survey. 815 questionnaires submitted online (Tencent Questionnaire) between 26 April and 3 May 2026, with the link forwarded by local government staff, who asked that their office and channels not be named; respondents answered on their own phones and staff had no access to the answers. Convenience sample; 84 submissions came from IP addresses in Liangshan Prefecture, 17 from elsewhere in Sichuan and 714 from outside Sichuan (released as a three-level variable). 73 coded variables, including five three-item Likert constructs (hazard concern, fire-duty burden, project participation, project dependence, perceived welfare) and four post hoc data-quality flags. Bilingual codebook and questionnaire text included. Code and outputs. Structural equation models with robustness checks, measurement-invariance and equivalence tests, and heterogeneity by IP location (R, lavaan); a Google Earth Engine pipeline for Landsat-only NDVI 2000–2025, a 200-basin donor pool, MODIS MCD64A1 burned area, FIRMS active fire, GLC_FCS30D land cover and CHIRPS/ERA5-Land climate; Python scripts for pixel-wise trends with FDR control, synthetic control / synthetic difference-in-differences with placebo inference, and fire activity relative to donor basins. Remote-sensing results. Growing-season NDVI rose across the watershed (median Sen's slope +0.0058 per year, 2000–2025), but no more than in 104 comparable basins: synthetic difference-in-differences estimate of the effect of the 2008 works −0.028 (95% CI −0.068 to 0.012, placebo p = 0.17). Version 2 corrects the description of how the survey data were collected, releases all 815 responses with collection date, completion time and IP-location group, replaces the version 1 remote-sensing files with the exports and outputs of a new Landsat-only pipeline, and corrects two specification issues of the version 1 SEM analysis. title: Mapping crown length and canopy depth across global forests at 1 km from multi-platform lidar and satellite data
description: Crown length (CL) describes the vertical extent of an individual tree's live crown. Canopy depth (CD) describes the vertical extent of the canopy within a forest stand. Both inform fire behaviour, vegetation and habitat models, yet their global distributions remain poorly resolved. We present global maps of mean CL and CD at 1 km resolution for 2020. We first retrieved CL for individual trees segmented from lidar point clouds, as tree height minus crown-base height. Within each of 1147 reference records on six continents, mean CL was the average of the tree values and CD was the 95th-percentile tree height minus the lowest crown base. Both were related to satellite and environmental predictors using random forest models. Tree-level CL agreed with field measurements and manual annotations with R² = 0.62 and RMSE = 2.63 m. Across 46 validation plots, RMSE was 1.90 m for mean CL and 2.09 m for CD. In the 30 % hold-out set, the mapping models achieved R² = 0.64 for CL and 0.72 for CD, with RMSE of 2.15 m and 2.98 m. Global mean CL and CD were 7.0 m and 14.2 m. Long crowns and deep canopies occurred in equatorial rain forests and humid temperate forests. Savannas, Mediterranean woodlands and dry forests had the smallest values. These maps give the first globally consistent view of the crown layer beneath the canopy top. They can constrain crown geometry in vegetation models, canopy fuel depth in fire models and vertical habitat structure in biodiversity studies.

title: Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance"
description: Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance" (Yiran Li), revision 1 (R1) of the manuscript under review at the Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies. This version supersedes version 1, which accompanied the original submission. The package contains the analysis code, the derived data tables and the figures underlying the paper, which presents a global source–receptor accounting of cross-border delta sediment starvation. Local sediment production is routed along the HydroBASINS river network; each dam's trapping is computed from its Brune efficiency and regulated-flow share; large natural lakes retain sediment with and without dams; natural loads are anchored to observed pre-dam values (39 rivers) or to the pristine loads of the Nienhuis et al. (2020) delta inventory; and each delta's dam-induced deficit is split into a domestic and a cross-border part and attributed to the upstream countries responsible. Key results (R1): dams withhold about 5,100 Mt yr⁻¹ of sediment from the world's inventoried deltas, of which about 1,130 Mt yr⁻¹ (22.1%) is withheld by dams in another country; 46 countries are net downstream bearers (25 of them bearing at least 1 Mt yr⁻¹); about 156 million people live on national delta parts that have lost at least a tenth of their sediment supply, mostly to foreign dams, 87% of them in Bangladesh and Egypt. Leading upstream sources: India, the United States, China, Ethiopia and Brazil. Contents: the analysis scripts (sediment_routing.py and the revision scripts run by run_all_r1.sh), the builders of the manuscript, Supplementary Material and response letter (build_all.sh), all derived CSV and JSON tables, Figures 1–5 and the graphical abstract. README_R1.md documents the input data, the run order, the method and all changes from version 1. A clean-room run from the public raw inputs (HydroBASINS, BasinATLAS, Global Dam Watch, the GlobalDeltaData of Nienhuis et al., the delta extents of Edmonds et al., the WorldPop 2020 grid, Natural Earth and World Bank GDP) reproduces every derived table byte for byte. The reviewer reports are confidential and are not included. No generative-AI tools were used to produce any figure or graphical artwork; all figures are data plots generated by the included code.

title: SOCOMv2: Experiment 2 (GOBM subsampling experiment) full experimental dataset
description: Dataset Information Current Version: v2 (changelog at end of repository Contacts: Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk) and Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) The Surface Ocean CO2 Mapping program entered its second phase (SOCOMv2) with a range of experiments which provides a coordinated, community-driven framework to evaluate surface ocean fugacity of CO2 in seawater (sfCO2) reconstructions and derived air–sea CO2 fluxes under present-day observational constraints. This repository holds the dataset used within a Global Ocean Biogeochemical Model (GOBM) subsampling experiment designated Experiment 2, where nine fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) reconstruction methodologies reconstructed five GOBMs from the Global Carbon Budget 2023 (and one from 2024). The analysis and results of the study are presented in Roobaert et al. (in prep). How to reference? If you use these data for a new analysis or publication, we request that you contact Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) and Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk). This will allow the authors, and the SOCOM community the opportunity to contribute and be considered for co-authorship, depending on their level of involvement. If these data are used please reference the orginial study (Roobaert et al. 2026) and the repository with the version. Data format This dataset includes five individual zip files which contain a single netCDF file. Within each netCDF, the model fCO2sw and air-sea CO2 fluxes alongside the sfCO2 reconstructions and resulting air-sea CO2 fluxes. Ancillary information including for example model sea surface tmeperature and salinity, gas transfer, wind speed and a consistent mask where all data products provide an fCO2 estimate, are included within each file to aid interpretation of the data. Each zip file contains a netCDF file with the corresponding naming: SOCOMv2_Ex2_<model_name>_full_variables_<version>.nc where <model_name> is the model name from the five models, and <version> represents the dataset version. Model naming is shown in the table below: Model Name CESM_ETHZ_r1 FESOM2_REcoM IPSL_r1 MRI_ESM2_2 NorESM_vGCB2024 We refer the user to the netCDF file for the full set of avaiable variables but as a quick start: Model fCO2 are found under: model_sfco2 Model air-sea CO2 fluxes are found under: model_flux The corresponding data product fCO2 and air-sea CO2 fluxes are found by replacing 'model' with the corresponding dataproduct name. title: A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes
description: A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes This dataset maps potential habitat within populated, human-used landscapes on a ~1 km² hexagonal discrete global grid (ISEA3H, resolution 16; 1.18491 km² cells). Spatial domain: all files cover the 114,791,301 land cells whose centroid lies at or north of 60°S. Antarctica and other land south of 60°S are not included. For each cell, the dataset provides: the cell centroid; country (FAO GAUL 2024, with de facto assignment for disputed areas); counts of 10 m land-cover pixels: Dynamic World 2024, ESA WorldCover 2021, Global Pasture Watch and the Spatial Database of Planted Trees v2.0; land area, habitat area and habitat fraction of land; population: WorldPop R2025A, 2024, 100 m; classification into 'Populated' and 'Shared' Landscapes. 'Populated Landscapes' are cells where more than 1% of land is non-habitat (crop, built-up, pasture or tree crops) and population density is at least 1 person per km² of land. 'Shared Landscapes' are Populated Landscapes in which at least 20% of land is habitat. Globally: Populated Landscapes cover 26.14 million km² (20.5% of land); Shared Landscapes cover 18.87 million km² (14.8% of land; 72.2% of Populated Landscapes); 37.75% of the population lives in Shared Landscapes. Files dgg_isea3h16_land_shapefiles.zip: the land grid as 377 zipped shapefiles (10° tiles). Cells touch Natural Earth 10m or OpenStreetMap land, with a 200 m buffer. dgg_cells_shared_landscapes_dataset.csv.gz: per-cell results: centroid, country assignment, pixel counts, population, land and habitat areas and fractions, and landscape classes (gzip CSV, 33 columns). dataset_summaries.zip: global_summary.csv and country_summary.csv, with areas, fractions and the fraction of population in Shared Landscapes. DATA_DICTIONARY.md: definitions of every column and file format. Code: https://github.com/njdepsky/SharedLandscapes (MIT). The grid script accepts any bounding box, for example a global grid. Article: Ellis et al., Data in Brief (2026). Licence and attribution: Open Database License (ODbL) v1.0. The grid is derived from OpenStreetMap data, © OpenStreetMap contributors. Dynamic World: "This dataset is produced for the Dynamic World Project by Google in partnership with National Geographic Society and the World Resources Institute." The inputs (Dynamic World, ESA WorldCover, Global Pasture Watch, SDPT v2.0, FAO GAUL 2024, WorldPop, Natural Earth) are used under their respective licences.

title: California Wildfire Perimeters with Environmental and WUI Attributes
description: This dataset contains processed fire perimeter records from four wildfire datasets: the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CalFire; 1990–2025), Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS; 1990–2024), the Global Fire Atlas (Atlas; 2001–2025), and the FIREDpy-based country-level dataset (FIRED; 2000–2024). Atlas and FIRED are derived from MODIS imagery. CalFire records are limited to fire events larger than 1 km². All four shapefiles include fire identifiers, ignition date, year and decade, burned area (size_km2), Northern/Southern California flags, and WUI classification attributes from intersecting fire perimeters with WUI boundaries (FireType: WUI vs Wildland; reachWUI; reachUrban). CalFire further includes containment date, ignition cause, climate and terrain variables (temperature, vapor pressure deficit, precipitation, wind, elevation, slope, NDVI, and land cover), ignition-based WUI classes derived by matching Global Fire Atlas ignition points to CalFire perimeters (IgnWUI; IgnType: WUIIgnite, WUISpread, or Wildland), the within-perimeter WUI burned-area fraction (WUIfrac), 4-day mean Canadian Fire Weather Index moisture codes (FFMC_4d, DMC_4d, DC_4d), Santa Ana wind occurrence flags for Southern California fires (SAW), and within-perimeter land-cover fractions from MCD12Q1 FAO-LCCS1 2020 (fracFor, fracGrass, fracShrub, fracSG). A full field list is provided in CalFire_added_fields.txt. The four perimeter datasets are provided as compressed Shapefiles. These data are intended to support research on fire size distribution, fire behavior, land-fire interactions, and WUI risk assessment.

title: Code and derived results: river-size association of Palaeolithic findspots in the Wainganga-Wardha basin, Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India
description: R code, unit tests, saved summary tables and figure-source tables for a spatial analysis of 197 Palaeolithic findspots (59 source references) in Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India (Wainganga-Wardha basin). The primary analysis estimates how site intensity varies with distance to drainage of increasing river size (WRIS stream order >= k, k = 3 to 9), using a down-weighted Poisson point-process likelihood with a ridge prior, spatial cluster-bootstrap inference, spatial cross-validation, a lineament-distance negative control and a robustness matrix. The analysis design was frozen and checksummed before the site-water models were fitted; the manifest is included. The primary hypothesis (intensity falls with distance to larger rivers) was not supported; the association depends on site classification, and exploratory analyses are labelled as such. Contents: scripts S01-S19, tests, saved result tables, figure-source tables, PDF figures, renv lockfile (R 4.5.2). Not included: exact site coordinates, the 1 km coarsened site table, and raw third-party data layers (WRIS, HydroRIVERS, ESA WorldCover, OpenStreetMap, Global Dam Watch), which must be obtained from their providers. Limitations: modern water bodies are a proxy for Pleistocene water; legacy survey bias; mixed coordinate quality; undated typology; no field validation.

title: Data and code for Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification
description: This archive contains the R code, dataset provenance, input-file fingerprints, summary data, validation outputs and reference figures supporting the study “Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification”. The analysis covers 2000–2020 at a 0.05-degree working grid and distinguishes five temporally stable vegetation classes. Ecosystem-stratified generalised additive models include site random intercepts and AR(1) errors. The primary model includes a spherical spatial smooth and CO2; a matched 2 × 2 design tests sensitivity to these two terms. Trend inference uses Newey–West standard errors and global Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Global and ecosystem summaries use actual pixel area, with spatial-block bootstrap intervals and spatial-block cross-validation. The archive includes pooled out-of-fold level, trend and sign diagnostics, area-representative held-out trend shares, five CO2 spatial-support scenarios, and machine-readable CSV versions of all 30 parts of Supplementary Tables 1–9. The environment–CO2 baseline and unexplained-residual shares are descriptive co-directional trend components. Their association with composite human pressure is exploratory and does not identify causal effects of human activity. Raw third-party datasets, high-resolution derived rasters, site-level source and prediction tables, and model objects are excluded where redistribution rights are unclear. Users must acquire source data from the official providers and follow the documented reconstruction workflow. The included Natural Earth coastline is public domain.
