title: AZ-Hydro — Historical and Projected Arizona Annual Water Use: Software, Input Data, Models, Raster and Well Package Predictions, and Validation at 2 km Resolution (1896–2099)
description: AZ-Hydro: Historical and Projected Arizona Annual Water Use, 1896–2099 (v1.2) A 2 km-resolution gridded dataset of Arizona groundwater and surface-water withdrawals, irrigation consumptive use, and pumping-induced stream capture, spanning 204 years (1896–2099), with per-pixel uncertainty from a six-component framework and a well-level package for ~170,000 registered consumptive wells. Companion data archive for Majumdar et al. (submitted to Nature Scientific Data; preprint https://doi.org/10.31223/X56N63) and Majumdar et al. (in prep., AGU Earth’s Future). Version 1.2 (code release v1.2.0). See What’s new in v1.2 below. What’s in this deposit File Size Contents Audience az-hydro-headline.7z ~8.7 GB Self-contained subset of every key output: six-band augmented per-pixel, per-year withdrawal, consumptive-use, and stream capture rasters (prediction, σ, CV, SNR, lower and upper 95 % CI); the GeoParquet well package; per-basin and per-sub-basin time series; the CAP shortage-scenario sweep; era-mean and trend figures; validation and intercomparison outputs. Most users want this. Reviewers and downstream users of the published product az-hydro-data.7z ~80 GB Full reproducibility archive (~220 GB uncompressed): everything in the headline archive plus the raw inputs, cross-validation outputs, intermediate input stacks, and per-component uncertainty rasters (σ_MACA, σ_model, σ_irr, σ_LULC, σ_GW, σ_USBR, σ_CU). Anyone re-running the pipeline from scratch az-hydro-1.2.0.zip ~64 MB Tagged source-code release (Python pipeline, GEE export and upload scripts, documentation), identical to the GitHub repository at tag v1.2.0. Anyone running the pipeline README.md, HEADLINE_README.md, ADWR_readme.txt ~50 KB Current copies of the guides inside the archives: Data/README.md (full archive), Data/HEADLINE_README.md (headline archive), and the ADWR folder’s readme.txt. They supersede the copies inside the .7z files, which predate the final author list and citations. Everyone Inside each .7z, Data/HEADLINE_README.md (headline archive) or Data/README.md (full archive) gives the per-directory inventory and the external-source citations. The standalone copies of these files in this deposit are the current versions. How to unpack the .7z files The archives use LZMA2 with solid-block compression, which macOS Archive Utility cannot open. Use one of: macOS: Keka or The Unarchiver Windows: 7-Zip, WinRAR, or Bandizip Linux: p7zip (for example apt install p7zip-full, then 7z x az-hydro-data.7z) What’s new in v1.2 Post-2026 Colorado River shortage. The central projection now uses the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines (U.S. Department of the Interior, August 2026), which reduce Arizona’s Colorado River apportionment by 760 kAF yr⁻¹ (CAP delivery factor 0.49, groundwater boost 7.5). The guidelines cover 2027–2028; 2029–2099 hold that latest official condition as a stand-in for continued shortage, not as a forecast. v1.0–v1.1 held the Tier 1 cut (512 kAF yr⁻¹) through 2099. Projected 2027–2099 groundwater withdrawal is 5.5 % higher and surface-water withdrawal 5.5 % lower than in v1.1; total withdrawal and all 1896–2026 predictions are unchanged. CAP scenario sweep. A ninth scenario applies the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines: 652 kAF yr⁻¹ of CAP delivery, the 900 kAF yr⁻¹ post-Tier baseline less the 248 kAF yr⁻¹ by which the guidelines’ 760 kAF yr⁻¹ Arizona reduction exceeds the Tier 1 cut that baseline is taken to include. It adds 1.30 MAF of groundwater pumping over 2027–2060 and 3.15 MAF over 2027–2099. The other scenarios are unchanged. Uncertainty ensemble. The ensemble members now apply the same dynamic CAP caps and floors as the central partition (a missing import had disabled them). σ for the groundwater and surface-water categories changes in every year; σ for total withdrawal does not. The scenario sweep keeps its full-delivery counterfactual. ADWR partner CSVs (Outputs/.../ADWR/). In v1.1, 14 of the 16 CSVs listed every basin-year twice, because the export also picked up the all-basin aggregate files. Each row now appears once, and Total_Predicted is built from the same per-basin series as the other categories, so Total_GW + Total_SW = Total_Predicted holds row by row. Basin totals count boundary pixels in every basin they touch, so summing basins exceeds the statewide total by about 2–3 %; statewide totals are in Annual_Summaries/. Headline archive now also includes the out-of-distribution probability rasters (OOD_Rasters/, 68 MB). GEE assets for the AZ-Hydro Explorer moved to projects/azhydro/assets/az-wu-v1-2/. Methods overview AZ-Hydro is a physics-constrained machine learning pipeline: XGBRF prediction of total annual withdrawal depth per 2 km pixel, trained on ADWR metered pumping records (1984–2024) with 22 predictors (actual and reference ET, precipitation, effective precipitation, temperature, land-cover fractions and densities, irrigated and groundwater-irrigation fractions, soil properties, water-table depth, well, surface-water-rights and canal densities, watershed streamflow, and pixel coordinates). Climate, ET, and land-cover inputs from different eras are joined into continuous 1896–2099 series by overlap-period bias correction. Density-ratio partition of the total into irrigation and non-irrigation withdrawals from groundwater and surface water, with consumptive use derived as CU = irrigation efficiency × irrigation withdrawal. The few free partition parameters were tuned to statewide USGS and ADWR records (USGS OFR 94-476, 1915–1990; USGS Circulars, 1950–2015; ADWR Annual Report totals and the 2019 ADWR shares); the machine learning totals are never adjusted. Six-component uncertainty quantification: σ_MACA (5 GCMs), σ_model (10 XGBRF seeds), σ_irr (irrigated-area input), σ_LULC (4 USGS land-use scenarios), σ_GW (5 recent well-registry snapshots), and σ_USBR (5 Upper Colorado River streamflow members), combined in quadrature and propagated to consumptive use (σ_CU). Stream capture index combining connectivity (exponential decay with water-table depth) and nearby surface-water availability, with pumping and connectivity uncertainty propagated to the capture volumes. Key validations Statewide agency reconciliation (calibration adequacy, not an independent test): 2017 ADWR total withdrawal 6.81 vs 7.00 MAF (−2.7 %); 2015 USGS groundwater withdrawal 2.96 vs 3.09 MAF (−4.1 %); 2019 ADWR irrigation share 74.2 % vs 72 %; 1955 and 1980 pumping peaks under-predicted by 6–11 %, with every reported total inside the model’s 95 % σ_total interval. Independent comparisons against USGS NHM withdrawals and consumptive use, USGS Reitz irrigation rasters, the USGS public-supply reanalysis, and CAP and SRP delivery records (statewide surface water within 0.8 % of the 1985–2024 CAP + SRP mean). WestWater Research (2026) CAP shortage anchor: Basic Coordination cumulative additional groundwater pumping 7.24 MAF over 2027–2060 vs 8.0 MAF (−9.5 %); Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF vs 8.7 MAF (the gap reflects AZ-Hydro’s no-regulatory-ceiling framing). CAP delivery shortage scenario sweep Nine scenarios (the no-cut Baseline_900kAF; DCP Tiers 0, 1, 2a, 2b, and 3; the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines; WestWater Basic Coordination; Extreme Shortage) re-partitioned over 2026–2099. Cumulative additional groundwater pumping over 2027–2060: Operating Guidelines 1.30 MAF, DCP Tier 1 4.05 MAF, DCP Tier 3 10.69 MAF, Basic Coordination 7.24 MAF, Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF. Basin and per-pixel maps, cumulative σ, and signal-to-noise figures are included for the 2027–2060 and 2027–2099 windows. External datasets required to reproduce the pipeline (not redistributed here) The pipeline reads four USGS ScienceBase data products that must be downloaded separately: USGS NHM withdrawals (Haynes et al. 2023): irrigation withdrawals and efficiency by HUC12, 2000–2020 USGS NHM consumptive use reanalysis (Martin et al. 2023; Martin et al. 2025): irrigation consumptive use by HUC12 USGS public-supply reanalysis (Luukkonen et al. 2023; Alzraiee et al. 2024): public-supply withdrawals by HUC12 USGS Reitz historical ET (Reitz et al. 2023; Reitz, Sanford & Saxe 2023): 800 m gridded ET Bundled here directly: ADWR Well Registry and metered pumping records, GW basin / AMA-INA / CAP / SRP / streamflow / USBR vectors, HarDWR water rights (Lisk et al. 2024), GRAIN canal network (Suresh et al. 2026), and the Ma et al. (2026) water-table depth. See Data/README.md inside each .7z for the exact file names and folders. title: Global gridded canopy height and height distributions from GEDI and ICESat-2 for EDv3 initialization at 0.01° resolution
description: This dataset provides gridded forest canopy structure inputs developed for the lidar-based initialization of the Ecosystem Demography model (ED v3.0), as described in Ma et al. (2023). It includes mean canopy height and canopy height histograms derived from NASA GEDI and ICESat-2 observations, together with tree canopy cover from the Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS), at a spatial resolution of 0.01°. These products characterize spatial variation in canopy height and the distribution of observed canopy heights within each grid cell. They were developed to connect satellite observations of forest structure with mechanistic ecosystem modeling and can support initialization and evaluation of other forest and vegetation models. Data contents The repository contains five GeoTIFF files: Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_avg.tif: Mean canopy height, in meters, calculated from filtered GEDI L2A version 002 RH100 observations. Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_hist_count.tif: GEDI canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell. Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_avg.tif: Mean canopy height, in meters, derived from filtered ICESat-2 ATL08 version 005 observations. Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_hist_count.tif: ICESat-2 canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell. CGLS_forest_percent_2019_001deg.tif: Tree canopy cover percentage for 2019, aggregated from the native 100 m CGLS product to 0.01°. Source observations and processing The study used GEDI observations acquired from March 2019 through August 2021 and ICESat-2 observations acquired from October 2018 through October 2021. GEDI observations cover approximately 51°S–51°N, while ICESat-2 provides observations beyond this latitude range. Observations were quality filtered and assigned to 0.01° grid cells. The filtering criteria documented in the paper were: GEDI: quality_flag = 1, sensitivity > 0.95, and RH100 > 5 m. ICESat-2: dem_removal_flag = 0, canopy_flag = 1, cloud_flag_atm < 4, and h_canopy > 5 m. Canopy height histograms contain 90 bins spanning 5–50 m at 0.5 m intervals. Each histogram layer records sample counts rather than normalized probabilities. Mean canopy height summarizes the retained observations within each grid cell. The products pool observations across the acquisition periods and do not represent annual time series. Use in model initialization In the associated study, canopy height histograms were used to index height-based lookup tables generated by ED v3.0. Model states associated with each height bin were weighted by the observed sample counts, preserving variation in canopy height within a grid cell. Tree canopy cover was then used to scale forest estimates to the whole grid cell. The histograms describe the distribution of sampled canopy heights across footprints or segments within a grid cell; they are not vertical foliage profiles or distributions of individual tree heights. Spatial coverage and sampling density vary because both lidar missions collect observations along orbital tracks. Cells without retained observations should not be interpreted as having zero canopy height. Associated publication Ma, L., et al. (2023). Spatial heterogeneity of global forest aboveground carbon stocks and fluxes constrained by spaceborne lidar data and mechanistic modeling. Global Change Biology, 29, 3378–3394. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16682 Please cite this dataset and the associated publication when using these products.

title: Ocean acidification and aragonite saturation, compounding anthropogenic stressors on marine life
description: Analysis scripts and derived data products behind the figures and numerical claims of Dryden & Duncan, "Ocean acidification, compounding anthropogenic stressors and marine water chemistry: evidence, regime-shift risk and implications for marine life". Contents: the winter aragonite threshold classification for all three zonation schemes; the same pipeline restricted to the polar and subpolar zone; the MODIS-Aqua equatorial Atlantic chlorophyll trend test; the figure build scripts; the derived 1-degree winter saturation and trend grids; the PyCO2SYS recomputation of aragonite saturation at the study sites with its per-point uncertainty; and the independent verification block. Primary datasets are not redistributed. OceanSODA-ETHZ v2025, SPOTS, GLODAP, CODAP-NA, World Ocean Atlas 2023 and the MODIS-Aqua ocean-colour products are public, carry their own DOIs, and are listed in README.md with the accessions needed to obtain them. Each script run against the original file reproduces the published values exactly. Expected outputs are tabulated in README.md so that any discrepancy is immediately visible. The polar-zone script deliberately reports the measured present state and no projection; the reason, a coverage artefact caused by seasonal ice in the trend mask, is documented in both the script header and the paper's Methods. Version 7 (October 2026) adds GOES_R1_graded_threshold_package.zip, the material behind the revised manuscript (revision R1 for BMC Marine Science): the graded ecological reference threshold (Omega 3.3 equatorward of 10 degrees to 1.6 poleward of 60 degrees), the winter aragonite saturation grids for 1982 to 2024 with the per-cell trend and the mask, the 1-degree block-mean MODIS-Aqua weights (net primary production, calcite and chlorophyll, 2019 to 2021) used to weight the water below its threshold, the month-by-month version of that weighting, the Monte Carlo, block-bootstrap and structural uncertainty with projections counted from 2023, the sea-surface-temperature variant of the threshold, and the scripts for Figures 1 to 3, S1 and S2 of the revised paper. Every script was re-run from the package before deposit: the numerical scripts reproduce the deposited results to rounding (two of them, run against the raw OceanSODA-ETHZ file, reproduce the deposited grids and JSON exactly), and the figure scripts reproduce the deposited PNG files byte for byte. title: GRedSIF: the first long-term harmonized global red solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset from the GOME-2 satellite series for 2007-2025
description: GRedSIF is a global monthly terrestrial red solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (RSIF) dataset derived from observations by GOME-2A, GOME-2B, and GOME-2C. It covers April 2007–December 2025 at a spatial resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°. RSIF values represent fluorescence at 683 nm and are expressed in mW m⁻² sr⁻¹ nm⁻¹. The dataset was generated through instrument degradation correction, robust principal component analysis (RPCA)-based radiance spectral denoising, singular value decomposition (SVD)-based RSIF retrieval, and zero-level bias correction. Cross-satellite differences were reduced using cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching, with GOME-2B serving as the reference. GRedSIF provides a harmonized, long-term RSIF record to support studies of vegetation photosynthetic activity, seasonal dynamics, interannual variability, and joint analyses of red and far-red SIF.
producing_institution: Aerospace Information Research Institute; University of Valencia

title: TROFSIF: A global full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset from TROPOMI enabled by radiance-spectrum denoising (Part 1: May 2018–October 2022)
description: This repository provides Part 1 of TROFSIF, a global Level-2 full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) dataset derived from TROPOMI observations, covering May 2018 to October 2022. The dataset provides footprint-level full-spectrum SIF observations over terrestrial ecosystems, including red (685 nm) and far-red (740 nm) fluorescence, retrieval uncertainties, and spectral parameters. The dataset contain two SIF basis coefficients that enable reconstruction of the complete fluorescence emission spectrum using the supplementary SIF basis spectra. Additional variables include geolocation, observation time, viewing geometry, and retrieval diagnostics. Daily HDF5 files are distributed in monthly archives. By providing multi-year global observations of both fluorescence magnitude and spectral characteristics, TROFSIF supports studies of vegetation photosynthesis, phenology, productivity, ecosystem stress, and terrestrial carbon-cycle dynamics. This repository constitutes Part 1 of the complete TROFSIF dataset spanning May 2018 to July 2026. Part 2, covering November 2022 to July 2026, is available in the companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23585026).

title: 202609 - Vessel detections from Sentinel 2
description: Vessel detections with Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from 2019 to 14 days ago. Multiyear detection of vessels with respective length, speed and orientation estimates based on deep-learning models applied to electro-optical imagery (RGB and near-infrared) at 10-m resolution covering most exclusive economic zones and marine protected areas across the ocean. Sentinel-2 detections are based on electro-optical imagery at 10-m resolution. Compared with our published Sentinel-1 detections based on SAR imagery at 20-m resolution, Sentinel-2 allows detecting smaller vessels with all types of vessel materials, in contrast with the weakness of SAR imagery on revealing vessels made of wood and fiberglass. Sentinel-2 also images the wakes of moving vessels, which further increase the detectability of small vessels and allow us to infer the vessels’ speed and orientation.The rich information contained in the optical imagery can be used to map not only vessel presence, but also vessel activities such as vessel encounters and bottom trawling. Sentinel-2 also covers more area of the ocean than Sentinel-1, and the novel neural-net detection approach does not require the exclusion of near-shore regions (as opposed to the CFAR approach), allowing detection of vessels in highly-packed areas all the way to the shoreline where most human activity is concentrated. Overall, with Sentinel-2 imagery we are able to detect about 3 times more vessels, “see” a broader range of vessel lengths and types, and infer more information of vessel activities than in our previous mapping using Sentinel-1 imagery.

title: WorldCereal crop calendars
description: This dataset contains the global crop calendar training and validation data used in the manuscript “Enhancing WorldCereal crop calendars with land surface phenology and machine learning” (Moletto-Lobos et al., 2026). It includes harmonized reference crop calendar points derived from GEOGLAM Crop Monitor, USDA-FAS, JRC ASAP, and FAO sources, together with phenology-based samples retrieved from MODIS Aqua NDVI Land Surface Phenology (LSP) time series and ERA5-Land climate variables. The dataset is organized into two main seasonal groups that follow the nomenclature used in the manuscript: S1 = Winter crops (equivalent to winter cereals in the paper) Includes reference and LSP-derived Start of Season (SOS) and End of Season (EOS) dates, including explicitly modeled dormancy periods. S2 = Summer crops (equivalent to summer cropping systems in the paper) Includes SOS and EOS samples for rainfed and monsoon-driven summer crops, corresponding to the “summer season” definition of the study.

title: ISOP synthetic ocean temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific, 2015
description: Daily ISOP (Improved Synthetic Ocean Profile) synthetic temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific (99°E–170°E, 20°S–66°N) for 1 January–31 December 2015. The product was developed by the authors following the methodology of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (Helber et al., 2013), with minor modifications. As described in the accompanying manuscript (Dan et al.), ISOP employs a three-layer vertical structure model (mixed layer, thermocline layer and deep quiescent layer) and uses a variational method combined with historical profile EOF statistics to project satellite sea surface observations onto the subsurface, generating three-dimensional temperature and salinity fields. Its satellite inputs are OISSTv2.1 daily 1/4° sea surface temperature, AVISO/DUACS global 1/8° multi-satellite merged sea surface height anomaly, and the Copernicus 1/8° sea surface salinity merged product. The product extends to a maximum depth of 1000 m (47 levels) at 1/4° horizontal resolution. Observational validation shows that its temperature and salinity errors are comparable to those of the HYCOM and GLORYS12V1 reanalyses, with grid-point temporal and daily spatial correlation coefficients of steric sea surface height with AVISO SLA of 0.874 and 0.897, respectively. The archive contains 365 daily NetCDF files named YYYYMMDD_isop.nc (20150101–20151231); temperature is in degrees Celsius and salinity in PSU, with missing values masked. Data are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Contact: Bo Dan (danb1991@163.com).

title: Earthen berm stochastic simulation (Landlab): code and data
description: Model code and simulation output for a global sensitivity study of earthen berms in dryland valleys. Each run is a 100-year Landlab simulation driven by CLIGEN storms for Tucson, Arizona, run once with a berm and once without it, using the same storms. The record contains the model (berm_driver.py) and the CLIGEN station file, end-of-run results and storm-by-storm series for a 1,152-run main ensemble, paired berm and no-berm storm records for 189 runs of an earlier per-storm ensemble, an older per-decile summary of 128 of those runs, the script that extracted the 189 runs from the raw output, and the raw output itself. README.md describes the files, and DATA_DICTIONARY.md describes every column.

title: Land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) data for the Global Carbon Budget 2026
description: Description This dataset provides estimates of net land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) and their component fluxes from the three bookkeeping models used in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026): BLUE (Hansis et al., 2015), LUCE (Qin et al., 2024), and OSCAR (Gasser et al., 2020). Peat drainage emissions are from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021), and peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). The dataset further includes the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026, including estimates from national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset also includes global and gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL), which is the difference in ELUC between a simulation with transient carbon densities and a simulation with pre-industrial carbon densities. The reported net ELUC estimates already include the environmental contribution (δL). Net ELUC and its component fluxes are available as global and national annual time series for 1850–2025. Net ELUC is also available as gridded annual time series (0.25° resolution) for 1959–2025. The data describe CO2 emissions and removals expressed as mass of carbon (C). For ELUC and its component fluxes, positive values denote emissions and negative values denote removals. The sign convention for δL is explained below. Empty cells in .xlsx files denote missing values. The dataset contains 20 files: One .xlsx file with global estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) Fourteen .xlsx files with country-level estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR, one for each of the net and component fluxes listed below (units: TgC/yr) Two NetCDF files with gridded net ELUC estimates for BLUE and LUCE (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) One .xlsx file with the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One .xlsx file with the global estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One NetCDF file with the gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) Global, country-level, and gridded data The dataset includes the following net and component fluxes. The identifiers shown in monospace are used in the corresponding country-level filenames and as worksheet names in the file with global estimates. “SC” denotes shifting cultivation, and “nonforest” refers to shrub and herbaceous vegetation: net-eluc (net ELUC): Net CO2 emissions from land-use change. clearing-allveg-total (deforestation and clearing of other vegetation (total)): Total CO2 emissions from deforestation and the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent clearing and clearing within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-allveg-total ((re-)growth of forest and other vegetation (total)): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of forests and shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent (re-)growth and (re-)growth within shifting cultivation cycles. wood-harvest-management (wood harvest & other management): CO2 emissions from the decay of harvested wood products and residues left on site, and CO2 removals through regrowth following harvest. cropland-pasture-urban (cropland-pasture-urban transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between cropland, pasture, and urban areas. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): CO2 emissions from peat drainage and anthropogenic peat fires. Peat drainage emissions are the average of estimates from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021). Peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation. clearing-forest-sc (deforestation in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from deforestation within shifting cultivation cycles. clearing-nonforest-permanent (permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 emissions from the permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation. clearing-nonforest-sc (clearing of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-forest-permanent (permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation): CO2 removals through forest growth and regrowth following permanent afforestation and reforestation. regrowth-forest-sc (forest (re-)growth in SC cycles): CO2 removals through forest regrowth within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-nonforest-permanent (permanent (re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation following permanent land-use changes. regrowth-nonforest-sc ((re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 removals through the regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. Components 2–6 sum to net ELUC (component 1). Components 7–10 are subdivisions of component 2 and sum to its total. Components 11–14 are subdivisions of component 3 and sum to its total. Environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) The environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) is defined as the difference in ELUC between simulations using transient and pre-industrial carbon densities (transient minus pre-industrial). Positive values indicate higher ELUC under transient carbon densities, and negative values indicate lower ELUC. Annual estimates are provided for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR in two files: GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_global_1850-2025.xlsx: Global estimates for 1850–2025 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr). GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_gridded_1959-2025.nc: Gridded estimates for 1959–2025 (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area). For OSCAR, country-level estimates were spatially disaggregated to a 0.25° grid using the spatial patterns of gross emissions and gross removals from BLUE (see Supplementary Section S.2.2 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Data underlying Figure 8 The file GCB2026_Figure8_Data.xlsx contains the datasets used in Figure 8 (a-c) of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr), within the period 1990–2025 for bookkeeping estimates and the sink in managed forests and for the period 2000–2025 for national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs; 2024 data replicated in 2025) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset groups and variables are as follows: Bookkeeping models (BMs) and peat datasets net-eluc (net ELUC): Component 1 in the above list. clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): Component 7 in the above list. other-transitions (other transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between shrubland, herbaceous vegetation, cropland, pasture, and urban areas, corresponding to the sum of components 5, 9, 10, 13, and 14 in the list above. forest (fluxes on forest land): CO2 fluxes on forest land, including permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation, net CO2 fluxes from shifting cultivation in forests, and net CO2 fluxes from wood harvest & other management, corresponding to the sum of components 4, 8, 11, and 12 in the above list. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): Component 6 in the above list. National greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) Inventory estimates are from Melo et al. (2026). net-lulucf-flux (net LULUCF flux): Net CO2 fluxes from land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires). Emissions from drainage of organic soils and fires on organic soils. other-transitions (other non-forest land uses): Net CO2 fluxes from cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements, and other land, including land remaining in these categories and transitions between them. Emissions from organic soils are reported under peat-emissions. forest (fluxes on forest land): Net CO2 fluxes from forest land remaining forest land and land converted to forest land, including harvested wood products and excluding organic soils. Dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) managed-forest-sink: The CO2 sink in managed forests estimated by DGVMs (see Supplementary Sections S.2.4 and S.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Atmospheric inversions net-lulucf-flux: The net LULUCF flux estimated by atmospheric inversions (see Supplementary Section S.2.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). title: The LULUCF Data Hub: translating global land use emissions estimates into the national GHG inventory framework (Version 4.1.0, 2026 NGHGI release)
description: This repository includes the data displayed in the LULUCF Data Hub, an online platform hosted by the EU Forest Observatory. It compiles various datasets of country-level CO₂ and non-CO₂ emissions and removals from land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF). The LULUCF Data Hub is described by Melo et al. (ESSD Discussion). The NGHGI LULUCF database is compiled and maintained by the European Commission (EC) Joint Research Centre (JRC) and was first described by Grassi et al. 2022. It includes CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes from LULUCF sourced from the National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (NGHGIs) submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), using methodologies established by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes reported by countries in IPCC categories and sub-categories are allocated to the classes Forest (excl. organic soils, excl. HWP), Deforestation (conversion of forest land to other land uses), Other non-forest land uses, Organic soils, and Harvested wood products (HWP) (see Box 1). In the LULUCF Data Hub, and through a multi-disciplinary collaboration, we show results from global key initiatives estimating anthropogenic land use GHG fluxes translated to conceptually align with NGHGI and IPCC Guidelines definitions. In version 4.1.0 we present CO₂ data from carbon cycle modelling (Global Carbon Budget, GCB 2026; Friedlingstein et al., ESSD Discussion), CO₂ and non-CO₂ data from Global Nature Watch (formerly Global Forest Watch, GNW 2026; update of Gibbs et al., 2025), and CO₂ data from EDGAR LULUCF (Rossi et al., ESSD Discussion). Data is available in Mt CO₂ yr⁻¹ and, where available, Mt CO₂e yr⁻¹. Net CO₂ fluxes include emissions by sources and removals by sinks; non-CO₂ emissions, where available, are reported separately. Countries are identified by their ISO3 code. In addition, the timeseries files also include aggregated estimates for World (WRD) and the European Union (EU27). Version 4.1.0 (NGHGI 2026 release) Contents Files made available in version 4.1.0 New in version 4.1.0 NGHGI database 4.1.0 Independent datasets translated to NGHGI/IPCC Guidelines definitions 4.1.0 Versioning and citation policy 1) Files made available in version 4.1.0 File Status vs. previous version timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv New data (NGHGI 2026 release), now covering 1990-2025, including CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes and, where available, the split of the FOREST class into FOREST_REMAINING and LAND_TO_FOREST; replacing v4.0.0 NGHGI content. timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv New data (NGHGI 2026 release) covering 1990-2025, with only the values actually reported by countries (not gap-filled) for CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes and, where available, the split of the FOREST class into FOREST_REMAINING and LAND_TO_FOREST; replacing v4.0.0 NGHGI content. timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026, 1990-2025, CO₂ only (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026, 1990-2025, CO₂ only (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. timeseries_GCB_spread_4.1.0.csv New file, not present in earlier versions: spread of the Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026 CO₂ estimates across the underlying bookkeeping models (BLUE, OSCAR, LUCE) and DGVMs (n=24), for both the original/reclassified and translated datasets, alongside the ensemble average, min/max and standard deviation reported in timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv. timeseries_GNW_original_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Nature Watch (GNW) 2026 (formerly Global Forest Watch), 2001-2025, now including non-CO₂ fluxes for the Forest and Deforestation classes (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. timeseries_GNW_translated_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Nature Watch (GNW) 2026 (formerly Global Forest Watch), 2001-2025, now including non-CO₂ fluxes for the Forest and Deforestation classes (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. text_box_iso3_4.1.0.csv Updated: discussion notes on the data by country, alongside data-source information. chart_sectors_4.1.0.csv Updated file replacing v4.0.0: all-sector (Energy, IPPU, Agriculture, LULUCF, Waste) summary from CRT Table 10s1/10s2, in both CO₂ and CO₂e (n=121 countries). managed_land_country_classification_4.1.0.csv Updated file replacing v4.0.0: per-country classification of the use of the managed land proxy (Decision tree A: use of managed land proxy; Decision tree B: treatment of CO₂ removals from forest land), used to inform the translation of the independent datasets to the NGHGI managed-land definition (see Figure 1 below). Includes area of managed and unmanaged forest reported to the UNFCCC in 2000, 2010 and 2020. 2) New in version 4.1.0 Extended time series (1990-2025) The NGHGI and GCB time series now cover the period 1990 (previously 2000) to 2025: timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv for NGHGI; timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv for GCB. Non-CO₂ fluxes The NGHGI and GNW datasets now also report non-CO₂ fluxes alongside CO₂: NGHGI identifies these via the new Gas column (CO₂, CO₂e, non-CO₂), and GNW adds them for the Forest and Deforestation classes only. timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv for NGHGI; timeseries_GNW_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GNW_translated_4.1.0.csv for GNW. Split of the Forest class Where available, the Forest class is further split into FOREST_REMAINING (forest land remaining forest land) and LAND_TO_FOREST (land converted to forest land), reported alongside FOREST (FOREST = FOREST_REMAINING + LAND_TO_FOREST where both are available; left blank where a country reports FOREST only — see Box 1): timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv. GCB model spread The new file timeseries_GCB_spread_4.1.0.csv reports the Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026 CO₂ estimates across the underlying bookkeeping models (BLUE, OSCAR, LUCE) and DGVMs (n=24), alongside the ensemble average, min/max and standard deviation already reported in timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv. 3) NGHGI database 4.1.0 Version 4.1.0 of the LULUCF Data Hub updates the NGHGI LULUCF database with data submitted to the UNFCCC up to August 2026 for the period 1990-2025. We provide data as submitted by countries in their inventories (timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv) and gap-filled without altering the levels and trends of the reported data (timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv). Gap-filling applies linear interpolation between reported years and flat extrapolation beyond the first or last reported year, independently for each country, category and gas; no values are generated where a country has not reported a given category at all. The completeness of LULUCF reporting in 4.1.0 is 95% (see Table 1 in read me file for data by class and region) and the proportion (%) of reported (not-gap-filled) LULUCF data in the NGHGI database 2000 and 2024 is 61.2% (see Table 2 and Table 3 in read me file for more complete results by decade and classes below) and ranges between 61.4% (Forest) to 83.3% (Organic soils). Version 4.1.0 of the NGHGI LULUCF database covers all 197 Parties to the UNFCCC, plus the EU27 aggregate. Each country's data is sourced from the most complete and recent submission available: GHGI 2026 from Annex I countries: 41 countries BTR1, First Biennial Transparency Report: 84 countries CRT extraction: 64 countries; BTR1/NID manual entry, for countries whose CRT is unavailable or in a non-standard format: 20 countries — Andorra (AND), Bangladesh (BGD), Bosnia and Herzegovina (BIH), Bolivia (BOL), Cambodia (KHM), Central African Republic (CAF), Cote d'Ivoire (CIV), Dominica (DMA), Israel (ISR), Kyrgyzstan (KGZ), Liberia (LBR), Madagascar (MDG), Montenegro (MNE), Nicaragua (NIC), Niger (NER), Pakistan (PAK), Papua New Guinea (PNG), Philippines (PHL), The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (MKD), Tunisia (TUN); BTR2, Second Biennial Transparency Report (CRT): 2 countries — Colombia (COL), Kazakhstan (KAZ); Pre-Paris reporting (National Communication, Biennial Update Report, REDD+, or NDC): 60 countries No LULUCF data available: 10 countries — Egypt (EGY), Kiribati (KIR), Libya (LBY), Maldives (MDV), Marshall Islands (MHL), Nauru (NRU), State of Palestine (PSE), Qatar (QAT), Sierra Leone (SLE), Holy See (VAT). Information on data sources and discussion on the data by country is available in the file text_box_iso3_4.1.0.csv. See also further information on data sources and completeness of the inventories in terms of classes reported in Table 1 in read me file. Version 4.1.0 flagged 8 countries as reporting implausible sinks in the Forest class (Table 4 in read me file) which Forest sinks summed together amount to -0.92 Gt CO₂ yr⁻¹ on average. 4) Independent datasets translated to NGHGI/IPCC Guidelines definitions 4.1.0 In version 4.1.0, the GCB and GNW (formerly GFW) datasets are updated to GCB 2026 and GNW 2026: timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv, timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv, timeseries_GNW_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GNW_translated_4.1.0.csv replace the corresponding v4.0.0 files with new 2026 data (1990-2025 for GCB; 2001-2025 for GNW, now also including non-CO₂ fluxes for the Forest and Deforestation classes), consistent with the Data Hub's versioning convention that x.1.x releases update all independent datasets. EDGAR LULUCF 2025 is unchanged, duplicated from version 4.0.0/3.1.2. 5) Versioning and citation policy The LULUCF Data Hub was pre-released during the IPCC Expert Meeting on Reconciling Anthropogenic Land-Use Emissions (IPCC, 2024; Grassi et al., 2025). Version 4.1.0 is a new release and complements earlier versions (3.1.2, 2.1.1, and 1.0.1). Current versions available: Version 4.1.0 (current): NGHGI 2026 (updated data: GHGI 2026 Annex I (41), 86 Biennial Transparency Reports (84 BTR1, 2 BTR2), and 60 pre-Paris reporting submissions; time series extended to 1990-2025 with non-CO₂ fluxes and the Forest-class split into Forest land remaining forest land / Land converted to forest land where available; cut-off date August 2026), GCB 2026, GNW (formerly GFW) 2026. Version 3.1.2: NGHGI 2025 (Version 2.1.1 complemented by Annex I 2025 GHG reporting, updated October 2025), GCB 2025, GFW 2025, EDGAR LULUCF 2025. title: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget
description: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget — 2026 Release This dataset provides gridded terrestrial biosphere model output from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional Scale Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, contributing to the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026). TRENDY is an international model intercomparison project that brings together simulations from dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) to investigate the global terrestrial carbon cycle and its response to environmental change, including atmospheric CO₂, climate variability and land-use change. This release contains the final gridded model output submitted for GCB2026. The simulations support the assessment of the global land carbon sink and analyses of terrestrial carbon fluxes, stocks and their variability. Experimental design and simulations The TRENDY-GCB2026 protocol comprises seven simulations (S0–S6) designed to investigate the effects of changing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, nitrogen deposition, climate and land use on the terrestrial carbon cycle. Simulations S4–S6 are introduced for the first time in GCB2026. The simulations differ in which environmental drivers vary historically and which are held at pre-industrial conditions: Simulation CO₂ / N deposition Climate Land use / N fertilisation S0 Fixed Fixed Fixed S1 Transient Fixed Fixed S2 Transient Transient Fixed S3 Transient Transient Transient S4 Fixed Fixed Transient S5 Transient Fixed Transient S6 Fixed Transient Transient Fixed conditions correspond to pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (year 1700), repeated early 20th-century climate (1901–1920), and pre-industrial land cover, wood harvest and nitrogen inputs, as applicable. Transient conditions follow historical changes in the corresponding drivers. Changes introduced in GCB2026 In previous Global Carbon Budgets, the land carbon sink (SLAND) was estimated primarily from S2, which assumes time-invariant pre-industrial land cover. This required a correction for sinks and sources on land subsequently converted to other uses. For GCB2026, three additional simulations (S4–S6) allow the land sink and its attribution to environmental drivers to be calculated using simulations with transient land cover. The land carbon sink is calculated as: SLAND = S3 − (S4 − S0) + δL where δL represents the transient environmental effects on land-use change emissions, estimated using bookkeeping models - and can be found at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902 The contributions from atmospheric CO₂ and nitrogen deposition and from climate are estimated as: CO₂ and nitrogen deposition: S3 − S6 + δL Climate: S3 − S5 + S0 These simulations provide a consistent framework for investigating terrestrial carbon fluxes under historical changes in environmental conditions and land use. Further methodological details are provided in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 Supplementary Information. Data availability Access and download the data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ The complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. The underlying NetCDF model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. This Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination The TRENDY-GCB2026 simulations were contributed by international modelling groups. The creators listed in this record include the TRENDY coordinators and a representative of each contributing model. TRENDY coordination: Stephen Sitch, Pierre Friedlingstein and Mike O'Sullivan. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. Release information This dataset corresponds to TRENDY version 15, the final version of the land model simulations used for the Global Carbon Budget 2026. Please use the naming convention "TRENDY-GCB2026" in publication/presentations. The Zenodo deposit contains the following files: trendy_listofvariables_GCP2026.xlsx — definitions and specifications of model output variables. TRENDY-GCB2026-manifest.csv — inventory of externally hosted gridded model output files, including filenames, paths, sizes and modification dates. TRENDY-GCB2026-model-credits.csv — contributing models, model representatives and TRENDY coordinators. TRENDY-GCB2026-data-policy.md — data usage, attribution and co-authorship requirements. The underlying gridded model output is hosted on Wasabi and is accessible through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. These model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. title: Zooplankton Samples Collected in the Bering Sea On Board the F/V Northwest Explorer from September to October, 2002
description: Zooplankton samples collected between September 8 and October 6, 2002 as part of the BASIS survey by the F/V Northwest Explorer . A total of 44 rope trawl stations were sampled along the Aleutian chain in the Bering Sea basin or within the proximity of the Aleutian Islands and stations on or adjacent to the Eastern Bering Sea shelf. Zooplankton were collected using a bongo net (mesh sizes: 333 and 505 microns) towed obliquely between the surface and 200 meters, or 20 meters from the sea floor. Zooplankton samples were split onboard the vessel with a Matoto splitter and sample halves were preserved in formalin and frozen. Formalin preserved specimens have been sent to the Polish sorting center for species identification; frozen specimens will be used for stable isotope analysis. Surface water samples were collected and filtered for stable isotopes, coccolithophores, and chlorophyll. Filters were frozen and 250 ml of the filtered water was retained for nutrient analysis (NO 2 , NO 3 , PO 4 , and SiO 3 ). [Reference: Murphy, J., N. Davis, O. Ivanov, M. Rohr, S. Elmajjati, and W. Barber. 2003. Cruise report of the 2002 F/V Northwest Explorer BASIS survey in the Bering Sea, September- October. (NPAFC Doc. 676 Rev. 1) 23 p. title: TROFSIF: A global full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset from TROPOMI enabled by radiance-spectrum denoising (Part 2: November 2022–July 2026)
description: This repository provides Part 2 of TROFSIF, a global Level-2 full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) dataset derived from TROPOMI observations, covering November 2022 to July 2026. The dataset provides footprint-level full-spectrum SIF observations over terrestrial ecosystems, including red (685 nm) and far-red (740 nm) fluorescence, retrieval uncertainties, and spectral parameters. The dataset contain two SIF basis coefficients that enable reconstruction of the complete fluorescence emission spectrum using the supplementary SIF basis spectra. Additional variables include geolocation, observation time, viewing geometry, and retrieval diagnostics. Daily HDF5 files are distributed in monthly archives. By providing multi-year global observations of both fluorescence magnitude and spectral characteristics, TROFSIF supports studies of vegetation photosynthesis, phenology, productivity, ecosystem stress, and terrestrial carbon-cycle dynamics. This repository constitutes Part 2 of the complete TROFSIF dataset spanning May 2018 to July 2026. Part 1, covering May 2018 to October 2022, is available in the companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23463271).

title: National Extraction-based CO2 Emissions
description: This is a draft release of annual national emissions accounts based on extracted fossil fuels and carbonates: emissions from oxidation of the fuels (or venting of fossil CO2) and decomposition of the carbonates (only in cement so far) are allocated to the country that extracted them regardless of where in the world oxidation / venting / decomposition occurs. These can be seen as a complement to territorial and consumption-based emissions (as well as emissions aligned with National Accounts). Estimates are derived from energy data published by the Energy Institute, Mohr et al. (2014), UN Statistics Division, JODI, and the Global Carbon Budget (for both flaring/venting and cement). Where available, national emissions are reported from 1850, while the per capita series starts in 1950. These start years may be pushed back to earlier periods in future releases. The final year of data is 2025. As a draft release, there are some issues with the estimates. For example, in some years the global total is less than the sum of the individual countries reported. Further, while the global totals are in general very close to the territorial emissions estimates in GCP's fossil CO2 dataset, there are some divergences. These things will be worked on as time permits.

title: Data and code for "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows"
description: # Data and code for "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows" Version 1.0 (2026-10-23) This archive contains all data products of the study "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows" and the code that produced them. Using SWOT lake observations densified with Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery, we observed storage changes at 1,447 reservoirs in 96 countries during 5,399 floods between August 2023 and August 2026, and corrected the bias from sparse satellite sampling with daily in-situ storage from the USA, Brazil and Australia. The median reservoir retained about one third of the flood inflow (corrected retention ratio 0.33; raw satellite lower bound 0.22). ## Contents ``` reservoir_flood_retention_v1.0.zip ├── README.md this file ├── dataset/ data products of the study (about 47 MB) │ ├── README.md field-by-field documentation │ ├── D1_flood_events.csv │ ├── D2_storage_series.zip │ ├── D3_pld_grand_map.csv │ ├── D4_calibration_pairs.csv │ ├── D5_cama_scenarios.zip │ └── D6_cama_obs_module.zip └── code/ full processing code and the data needed to redraw the figures (about 82 MB) ├── README.md workflow and usage ├── LICENSE ├── scripts/ ├── data/ └── figures/ ``` ### dataset/ | File | Content | |---|---| | D1_flood_events.csv | Flood-event retention dataset (core product): 5,399 floods × 88 fields, including raw and corrected retention ratios, pre-flood headroom, GloFAS reservoir-module retention and reservoir attributes | | D2_storage_series.zip | Reservoir storage time series: SWOT-only (3,033 reservoirs) and SWOT + optical fused (2,938 reservoirs) | | D3_pld_grand_map.csv | Lookup between the SWOT Prior Lake Database and GRanD: 12,729 lakes matched to 6,719 reservoirs | | D4_calibration_pairs.csv | Satellite–in-situ calibration pairs: 732 floods at 171 reservoirs | | D5_cama_scenarios.zip | CaMa-Flood v4.3 results for seven reservoir scenarios at dam sites and downstream | | D6_cama_obs_module.zip | Observation-constrained CaMa-Flood reservoir module (Fortran), daily input tables and run scripts | D2, D5 and D6 are themselves zip files because they contain many files or large tables; unzip them where needed. See `dataset/README.md` for every field. ### code/ Scripts for the full workflow, in eight steps: | Folder | Step | |---|---| | scripts/01_swot | SWOT download, lake–reservoir matching, storage series, water-level validation | | scripts/02_optical | Sentinel-2/Landsat water-area extraction and fusion with SWOT | | scripts/03_glofas_events | GloFAS inflow, return periods, flood event detection | | scripts/04_insitu | In-situ data download (USACE CWMS, BoM, ONS) and in-situ checks | | scripts/05_calibration_drivers | Bias correction and analysis of controlling factors | | scripts/06_cama | CaMa-Flood forcing, observation-constrained module, scenario runs and comparison | | scripts/07_figures | Main figures | | scripts/08_release | Dataset release package | `code/data/` contains the inputs needed to redraw the four main figures. To redraw them: ```bash cd code/scripts/07_figures python fig_main_v8.py ``` The output PNGs are byte-identical to the figures in the paper. See `code/README.md` for the full workflow, the software environment (Python 3.9; gfortran for CaMa-Flood) and the raw data that must be downloaded separately (SWOT, GloFAS, ERA5-Land; several hundred GB in total). ## How the two folders relate - `dataset/` holds the final data products; `code/` holds the scripts that produce them and a copy of the intermediate tables needed for the figures. - `code/scripts/08_release/make_release.py` builds the files in `dataset/` from the full working data. - The Python scripts and run scripts inside `dataset/D6_cama_obs_module.zip` are identical to those in `code/scripts/06_cama/`. - All tables are linked by the GRanD reservoir identifier `GRAND_ID`; flood events are identified by `event_id` (`GRAND_ID_peakdate`). ## Main caveats 1. The bias correction is trained on in-situ data from the USA, Brazil and Australia only; applying it elsewhere is an extrapolation. The raw satellite retention ratio (`ret_wm`) is provided as a lower bound. 2. Single-event corrected retention ratios are uncertain; aggregate by reservoir, region or group. 3. All analyses use SWOT observations with quality flag good (quality_f = 0). The SWOT-only series in D2 also keep suspect observations (quality_f = 1), which should normally be removed. 4. In-situ reservoir records from USACE, ONS and BoM, and the flood storage capacity estimates of Shen et al. (2025), are not redistributed. ## Licences | Part | Licence | |---|---| | Data in `dataset/` and `code/data/` | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) | | Scripts written for this study in `code/scripts/` | MIT (`code/LICENSE`) | | Files derived from CaMa-Flood (`code/scripts/06_cama/fortran/`, `code/scripts/06_cama/gosh/`, and the module and run scripts in D6) | Apache License 2.0, as the original CaMa-Flood code (licence text in `code/scripts/06_cama/LICENSE-Apache-2.0.txt` and in D6) | Third-party sources must also be cited under their own terms: SWOT LakeSP (doi:10.5067/SWOT-LAKESP-D), GloFAS v4 and ERA5-Land (Copernicus), GRanD and Global Dam Watch, GRDL (doi:10.1029/2023WR035781), GROWL (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31225405), Sentinel-2 and Landsat, and the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators.

title: SeaWiFS Data by NASA Goddard
description: Consists of satellite measurements of global and regional ocean color data obtained by the Sea-viewing Wide Field-of-view Sensor, in orbit on the OrbView-2 (formerly SeaStar) platform. The concentration and predominant identity of substances and particles in the euphotic (lighted) zone of the upper ocean influences the apparent color of the ocean, which can range from deep blue to varying shades of green and ruddy brown. Living phytoplankton (which contain chlorophyll and associated photosynthetic pigments), inorganic sediments, detritus (particulate organic matter), and dissolved organic matter all contribute to the color of the ocean. The data are primarily intended for used by marine researchers. All SeaWiFS data files are in Hierarchical Data Format (HDF). [ Reference: PICES Scientific Report No. 18 2001, Proceedings of the PICES/CoML/IPRC Workshop on "Impact of Climate Variability on Observation and Prediction of Ecosystem and Biodiversity Changes in the North Pacific", http://www.pices.int/publications/scientific_reports/Report18/default.aspx. ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

title: Nimbus-7 Coastal Zone Color Scanner (CZCS) Data
description: A global ocean color data set derived from satellite observations. In most oceanic regions, the color of the ocean is primarily determined by the abundance of phytoplankton and their associated photosynthetic pigments. As phytoplankton pigment concentration increases, ocean color gradually shifts from blue to green. NASA developed the CZCS to utilize this characteristic of ocean color for the observation of pigment distribution in the oceans. The CZCS was launched on the Nimbus-7 satellite in October 1978. During the 91 months of its operation (October 1978 - June 1986), CZCS acquired nearly 68,000 images, each covering up to 2 million square kilometers of ocean surface. Data can be obtained directly at ftp://daac.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/czcs. title: Downscaled GRACE Total Water Storage Change (TWSC) Dataset on a 1 km grid at daily intervals for Naryn – Kara Darya basins and Fergana valley (2002–2023)
description: This dataset contains daily estimates of terrestrial water storage changes (TWSC) derived from the downscaling of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) observations over the Naryn–Kara Darya basins and the Fergana Valley in Central Asia. The dataset covers the period from 1 April 2002 to 31 December 2023 and is provided on a 1 km grid. The downscaling is performed by integrating GRACE/-FO data with hydrological forcing datasets, including precipitation, evapotranspiration, and river discharge from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP), the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and the Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS), respectively. The dataset is produced in support of a forthcoming manuscript on GRACE downscaling and terrestrial water storage dynamics in Central Asia. The final version will be uploaded after peer review. Variables: - twsc — daily terrestrial water storage change, expressed as equivalent water height in mm/day; dimensions: (time, lat, lon). - lat — latitude of grid-cell centres, in degrees north. - lon — longitude of grid-cell centres, in degrees east. - time — days since 1970-01-01 00:00:00, with daily timestamps at 12:00.

title: One island, three countries: aquaculture ponds explain the cross-border gap in mangrove loss on Borneo
description: Borneo's mangroves share one coastline, one climate and one sediment regime, yet they are governed by three countries. Using the annual Global Mangrove Watch v4.1 series and open data, this study asks why mangrove in Indonesian Kalimantan is lost faster than in Malaysian Borneo and Brunei, and tests three explanations: protected-area performance, conversion pathways and El Niño sea-level fall. Between 2010 and 2020, Kalimantan lost 1.23% of its mangrove a year, against 0.43 to 0.74% in Malaysian Borneo and 0.50% in Brunei; it held 59% of the island's mangrove and 77% of its gross loss. Matched comparisons show long-standing strict protected areas reduced loss in Malaysian Borneo by about 2 percentage points but had no detectable effect in Kalimantan. Protection nonetheless explains little of the gap: 84% of it arises in unprotected mangrove, and Sabah's 2015 upgrades of low-loss production reserves to full protection added nothing measurable. Classifying what replaced mangrove lost from 2000 to 2024 shows that conversion to aquaculture ponds, concentrated in the early 2000s, accounts for all of Kalimantan's 15.9-point excess loss, while loss away from ponds was similar in total on both sides of the border (clearing in Kalimantan and Sarawak, mostly edge change in Sabah) and oil palm replaced little mangrove. Annual loss outside conversion was lowest in El Niño years and highest in high-sea-level years, consistent with humid mangroves buffered against El Niño sea-level fall. Reducing Borneo's mangrove loss therefore depends on governing pond expansion in unprotected mangrove more than on adding protected areas. title: Monthly Global LAI and FAPAR with Mapped Managed Land Excluded, 1982–2024 (0.25°)
description: This dataset contains monthly global leaf area index (LAI) and fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR) from January 1982 to December 2024 at 0.25° resolution. The source data are harmonized AVHRR–MODIS vegetation records described by Jeong et al. (2024, 2026). Four static masking scenarios exclude mapped managed land, pasture-associated areas, water, and permanent snow or ice. Three CCI-based masks identify 0.05° cells where the ESA-CCI/C3S managed-cover fraction reaches α = 0.05, 0.10, or 0.20 in at least three annual maps. The GLC-based mask identifies 0.05° cells classified as cropland or urban in at least three GLC_FCS30D observations. All scenarios also exclude areas where LUH2 pasture overlaps mapped grass cover. The masks are applied at 0.05° resolution before area-weighted aggregation to 0.25°. Each 0.25° value is the area-weighted mean of its valid retained 0.05° subcells. Areas retained after masking have lower mapped managed-land influence according to the selected datasets and masking criteria. The four scenarios represent alternative retained spatial domains. Two ZIP archives contain 516 monthly GeoTIFF files for each masking scenario and vegetation variable. The files use the EPSG:4326 coordinate reference system. title: Code and derived data for "Cascading vulnerability in the Limboto Basin, Gorontalo"
description: This repository accompanies the article "Cascading Vulnerability in the Limboto Basin, Gorontalo: Dry-Season Drought, Tree-Cover Loss, and Vegetation, Lake, and Rice Responses, 2001–2025" by Pramono Putra S. Pido (Department of Geography, Universitas Indonesia). The article tests whether dry-season drought amplified by El Niño propagates from rainfall to soil moisture, vegetation, tree cover, Lake Limboto, and rice production in Gorontalo Province, on the northern arm of Sulawesi, Indonesia. The analysis compares three non-overlapping zones within the province (the North zone, the South zone, and the Limboto Basin) and also covers the province as a whole; tree-cover loss is examined in the HydroBASINS level 8 watershed unit that contains Lake Limboto and in the province. The analysis combines openly available satellite, reanalysis, and climate-index data with official rice statistics: CHIRPS v2.0 rainfall, expressed as the 1- and 3-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-1 and SPI-3), and ERA5-Land soil moisture and skin temperature for 1981–2025; GPM IMERG rainfall and SMAP L4 soil moisture as comparison products; the MODIS Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI) for 2001–2025, computed with and without pixel-quality filtering; Hansen Global Forest Change v1.12 tree-cover loss and ESA WorldCover 2021 at 30 m; FIRMS active-fire detections on a 1 km grid and MODIS MCD64A1 burned area; the water area of Lake Limboto from JRC Global Surface Water (1984–2021) and Sentinel-2 (July–October, 2019–2025); MODIS EVI over cropland in the Limboto Basin (2018–2024); the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), the monthly Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly, and the Dipole Mode Index (DMI); and rice harvested area, yield, and production for 2018–2025 from BPS-Statistics Indonesia and BPS-Statistics of Gorontalo Province. The Python scripts compute July–October (dry-season) composites; lagged correlations with an effective sample size, prewhitened cross-correlations, and bidirectional Granger causality tests, including conditional tests, along the monthly chain from rainfall to soil moisture to vegetation; correlations, partial correlations, and Granger tests between the climate indices and SPI-1; zone-specific regressions of the vegetation indices on SPI-3 and a pooled Zone × SPI-3 model with standard errors clustered by year; comparisons of tree-cover loss between dry-season drought years and other years; a two-way (cell and year) fixed-effects model that relates the tree-cover loss rate of 1 km cells to active-fire detections, together with a partition of the excess loss in dry years between fire-detected cells and cells without fire detections; annual summaries of the water area of Lake Limboto; summaries of rainfall, soil moisture, and cropland EVI by cropping-season window, set against the rice statistics; and a simulation of the effect of the ONI running mean on the Granger test. The archive Limboto_cascading_vulnerability_v1.0.zip contains the Google Earth Engine scripts that extract the satellite and reanalysis data; the Earth Engine exports and the small external input files used in the reported run; the Python scripts that compute the numbers, tables, and figures reported in the article and its Supplementary Material; the outputs of that run; Figures 1–10 in English and Indonesian; and a manifest that lists the size and SHA-256 checksum of every file. The README, which is also provided as a separate file, gives the order in which the scripts are run and links each table and figure in the article to its output files. The station data, the publications read by two of the scripts, and the FAO GAUL boundaries and the zone polygons derived from them are not redistributed; the README explains how to obtain or recreate them. The code is released under the MIT License. The README, the results, the figures, and the Earth Engine exports are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0), without prejudice to the terms of the source datasets; the files in data/external/ remain under their providers' terms.

title: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - Models and data sets for the ocean sink estimate in the Global Carbon Budget
description: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - 2026 Release This dataset provides surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs), surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products) and the ocean inverse model OCIM (interior ocean observationally-constrained estimate). Types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series (2) one file per GOBM and simulation (A, B) with gridded fields (3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations (4) the gridded file of the natural steady state fluxes from simulation B of six GOBMs that exclude riverine fluxes and have a globally-integrated natural steady state CO2 flux within ± 0.2 GtC yr-1. This data is used to subtract the natural steady state fluxes from the fCO2-products in regional anaylses (Figures 14 and 15) (5) A file for the gridded CO2 fluxes and one file for the global time-series of the ocean inverse model OCIM (simulations C and B) that is used as an observationally-constrained interior ocean data-product in GCB. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2026, are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 spreadsheet (https://globalcarbonbudget.org/datahub/). The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2026 paper, the river flux adjustment needs to be added and an adjustment for the natural steady state fluxes needs to be subtracted from the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (River flux adjustment: North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2026 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. Three of the ten fCO2-products (UExP-FFN-U, JMA-MLR and AOML-ET) include a temperature adjustment to correct the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803). Model simulations: Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability) Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability) (1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly): fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south (2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields. Temporal resolution: monthly. Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) are saved in separate files. fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude (3) One file 'GCB2026_GOBMs_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc' with the globally and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs,for simulations A, B, C and D. We also report an adjusted global time-series of simulation A that accounts for model drift (Aadj). Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual. (4) One file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_1959_2025.nc) that contains the gridded field and one file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc) that contains the global time-series of CO2 fluxes of OCIM for simulations C and B. Further data availability: Access and download the additional data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ In addition to the zenodo deposit, the complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. In addition to the data described above, this Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination: The GCB2026-OCEAN data sets were contributed by international research groups. The creators listed in this record include the GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators and a representative of each contributing data set. GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators: Judith Hauck and Peter Landschützer with support from Simone Le Chevère and Alizée Roobaert. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. How to cite this dataset When using the GCB2026-OCEAN data, users should cite both of the following resources: Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the ocean carbon sink. GCB2026-OCEAN dataset: Hauck et al. Users intending to use the model output in research or publications should consult the data policy and contact the GCB-ocean coordinators and relevant modelling groups as appropriate. The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence associated with this Zenodo record applies to the data deposited here. It does not apply to the additional gridded model output hosted externally on Wasabi, for which the GCB-OCEAN data policy governs use and redistribution. The data policy and additional model output can be accessed through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ Related publication Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data, https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2026-895 Global Carbon Budget 2026 synthesis data The official Global Carbon Budget 2026 data supplement, including the global carbon budget spreadsheet containing aggregated ocean carbon sink estimates derived from the GOBM and fCO2-product ensembles, is available through the ICOS Carbon Portal: https://www.icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2026 The ICOS data supplement and the GCB-OCEAN gridded model output are complementary resources. title: Data and code for: Land-cover product choice alters assessments of urban riverfront change: Evidence from four Chinese cities
description: This dataset contains the data and analysis code supporting a comparison of CLCD v1.0.5 and GLC_FCS30D v2 along urban riverfronts in Fuzhou, Guangzhou, Hangzhou and Nanning, China. The study uses the 2010 and 2020 classifications for one predefined 15 km main-river reach in each city. The files include land-cover windows, frozen study geometries and class mappings, pixel- and edge-level records, derived tables, GIS layers, and source code. The analyses cover product-specific land–water interfaces, strictly paired interface states, and land-cover transitions in two landward distance bands. Supplementary workflows examine common source classes, proximity between interfaces, reference water geometry, leave-one-segment-out sensitivity, and half-cell shifts of the analysis grid. Figure source data and the submitted supplementary tables are also included. The historical-imagery records contain the acquired Landsat and Sentinel windows, source metadata, archived AI observations, and eligibility decisions. No two-date trajectory met the predefined main-reference criteria; these records therefore do not provide an independent estimate of either product’s accuracy. The README identifies the calculation entry points and software requirements. File checksums and execution records document the archived inputs and the checks performed when preparing this deposit. Third-party data retain their original licences and source attribution.

title: Zambia Decoupling Dataset, 1950–2024: Annual Emissions, Economy, Energy and Land-Use Indicators
description: The Zambia Decoupling Dataset 1950–2024 is an annual country-level time series for Zambia. It has 75 rows, one per year from 1950 to 2024, and 62 columns, in a CSV of about 29 KB. It was assembled to test whether Zambia’s economic growth has been decoupled from its carbon emissions. It brings together fossil, cement and land-use CO₂, primary energy, electricity generation by source, population, GDP and forest area. Sources are the Global Carbon Budget 2025, Jones et al. via Our World in Data, the Energy Institute and EIA, Ember, World Bank World Development Indicators via Gapminder, the Maddison Project 2023 and FAO’s Forest Resources Assessment 2020. Beyond the copied series, the file includes per-capita and intensity indicators, and a set of exploratory electricity-sector CO₂ estimates built on assumed emission factors. The manuscript does not use those estimates. Coverage differs by variable and thins out in 2023–24, and blank cells are gaps rather than zeros. The main caveats are that land-use CO₂ is model-based and uncertain, that primary energy excludes traditional biomass, and that the 2024 hydro value is provisional. The GDP series also differ between Maddison and the World Bank, so use one series per analysis. The full variable dictionary and handling guidance are in the data description doc.

title: Global 0.1° Monthly Anthropogenic CO₂ Emissions Dataset with Near-Real-Time Updates
description: This dataset provides global monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°, with the latest update extending through September 2026. The dataset is designed to provide a valuable resource for assessing the global carbon budget and the effectiveness of climate mitigation efforts. The estimates are generated using a deep learning–based framework that employs a convolutional neural network as its backbone and incorporates a mask fusion module to address spatially missing input data. The framework integrates satellite observations, meteorological reanalysis data, and temporal and spatial encoding features to estimate anthropogenic CO₂ emissions at a global scale. The data are provided in NetCDF format on a global 0.1° × 0.1° grid (1800 × 3600 cells) using the WGS84 geographic coordinate system. Each file contains monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates for all 12 months of a given year, expressed in tonnes month⁻¹ cell⁻¹. Files follow the naming convention ACO2_01deg_YYYY.nc, where YYYY denotes the corresponding year. The dataset is also updated regularly at doi: 10.12237/casearth.6a01788fe8a21d1686165027 A manuscript describing the methodology and dataset is in preparation.
