title: Physics-Guided Multi-Fidelity Surrogate and Regime-Aware Evolutionary Optimization for Climate-Adaptive Eco-Hydrological Wetland Restoration
description: Overview This record contains the de-identified eco-hydrological restoration benchmark used to evaluate PG-RAMEO (Physics-Guided Regime-Aware Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization), a surrogate-assisted many-objective framework for climate-adaptive wetland restoration. The benchmark couples two-dimensional Saint–Venant shallow-water hydrodynamics with multi-decadal vegetation, salinity and soil-organic-carbon succession across 240 wetland restoration units spanning three geomorphological archetypes (Floodplain Marsh, n = 96; Coastal Estuarine, n = 84; Depressional Peatland, n = 60) under three hydro-climatic forcing regimes (Historical, CMIP6 SSP2-4.5, CMIP6 SSP5-8.5). Source data and de-identification. Hydrological boundary conditions, bathymetric depths, porewater salinity gradients and archetype proportions are anchored to three public monitoring repositories: the USGS Everglades Depth Estimation Network (EDEN) and NWIS (sofia.usgs.gov/eden, waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis), the CAMELS catchment dataset (ral.ucar.edu/solutions/products/camels), and the Global Lakes and Wetlands Database GLWD v2 / HydroSHEDS (hydrosheds.org/products/glwd). All station identifiers and geographic quasi-identifiers have been replaced by randomized hash codes (WRU_xxxx), calendar dates are omitted, and the spatial partition is encoded in the split column (train = 144, val = 36, test = 60). Contents data/processed/ — granular evaluation records (8 files, 8,315 data rows): wetland_basins_metadata.csv — 240 rows. Physical, hydrological and biogeochemical attributes of every restoration unit: area, drainage area, cell count, control structures, inflow, mean depth, hydroperiod, reference evapotranspiration, salinity, initial biomass, soil organic carbon, Manning roughness, bathymetric discontinuity, critical salinity (22.5 ppt) and anoxic (42.0 d) thresholds, and sensor missing rate. method_basin_regime_evaluations.csv — 5,760 rows (240 units × 3 regimes × 8 methods). Four-objective hypervolume (hv), igd_plus, candidate and feasible counts, ecological regime violation counts by mechanism (salinity_violations, anoxia_violations, desiccation_violations), surrogate state errors (rmse_h, rmse_biomass, mass_balance_err), individual objective scores (obj_hsi, obj_ncsr, obj_faee, obj_lcec), and computational speedup. seed_level_test_runs.csv — 720 rows (30 seeds × 3 regimes × 8 methods) on the held-out test split, the input to all paired significance tests. ablation_basin_evaluations.csv — 1,440 rows across the eight variants (Full, Abl-C1, Abl-C1b, Abl-C2, Abl-C2a, Abl-C2b, Abl-C3, Backbone). surrogate_operator_grid.csv — accuracy and mass-balance consistency of seven neural and statistical operator architectures. sensitivity_sweep_grid.csv — sweeps over flux weight λflux ∈ [0.0, 2.0], high-fidelity query ratio ρHF ∈ [0.05, 0.20], repair step ηrep ∈ [0.02, 0.40] and solver budget BHF ∈ [60, 480]. pareto_front_solutions.csv — representative non-dominated solutions per method. regime_shift_trajectories.csv — monthly coupled state trajectories (S(t), h(t), B(t)) over a 36-month SSP5-8.5 compound drought–flood sequence, comparing unrepaired offspring, random-mutation repair and CR-FEH directional physics-Jacobian repair. data/derived/ — the summary tables behind every reported result (7 files, 182 rows): main_table.csv (primary comparison on val and test), regime_archetype_table.csv (subgroup breakdown), ablation_table.csv, surrogate_consistency_table.csv, sensitivity_table.csv, dataset_summary_table.csv, and failure_mode_breakdown.csv (violation counts by physical failure mechanism under SSP5-8.5). Every file in data/derived/ is regenerated deterministically from data/processed/ by the companion code record. Reuse Released under CC BY 4.0. If you use these data, please cite this record together with the associated article. The columns obj_hsi, obj_ncsr, obj_faee and obj_lcec denote habitat suitability index, net carbon sequestration rate, flood attenuation efficiency and lifecycle engineering cost respectively; ehr_fr is the ecological regime feasibility ratio.

title: Harmonised fractional land cover time series for the Mediterranean region derived from ESA CCI LC and GLC_FCS30D

Each valid grid cell contains class-specific fractional cover values between zero and one, describing the mapped composition rather than a single dominant class. title: A 1-km monthly surface air temperature dataset for Arctic land (2000–2025)
description: Monthly mean near-surface (2 m) air temperature at 1-km resolution over Arctic land for March 2000 to December 2025 (310 monthly fields), reconstructed by an ensemble of Random Forest, LightGBM and XGBoost regressors trained separately for each calendar month on station observations (CRUTEM5 station archive, release 5.1.0.0) with MODIS predictors: Terra and Aqua day-time and night-time land surface temperature (MOD11A2, MYD11A2), Terra and Aqua NDVI (MOD13A3, MYD13A3), MCD12Q1.061 LC_Type5 land-cover fractions, latitude and longitude. Elevation is deliberately not a predictor; the reasons, and the measured consequence, are given in the accompanying paper. What changed in version 3.0. The predictor values of the training table are now pooled from the same gridded stacks the prediction reads, rather than from a separate extraction of the granules, so that training and prediction use one source. The land surface temperatures entering training are screened with three checks of the GHCN-Daily quality-assurance system at their published thresholds (world-record exceedance, a climatological outlier check at six biweight standard deviations, and spatial corroboration against the nearest neighbours); 3860 values, 0.50 % of the land surface temperatures, were found to be invalid — seven satellite month-year composites had reached the table with MODIS fill values that had not been masked when the monthly means were formed — and are treated as missing. The gridded predictor stacks were checked for the same signature and carry none of it, so no field of version 2.0 was affected by that defect. The models were refitted and the whole record re-predicted. Hold-out accuracy at the 120 withheld stations improves from 1.50 to 1.48 °C root-mean-square error. Data are on the native MODIS 1-km sinusoidal grid (34 tiles h09–h26, v00–v02, mosaicked to 3600 × 21600 cells, pixel 926.625433 m) with 2-D latitude/longitude and a CF grid mapping, so no resampling has been applied to the values. Water pixels are removed with the MOD44W mask and Greenland is excluded. Each annual file (ArcticSAT1km_monthly_YYYY.nc, CF-1.8 netCDF4) contains: sat — monthly mean near-surface air temperature (°C), ensemble mean of the three models; sat_model_spread — the per-pixel standard deviation of the three individual model predictions for the same month, a measure of structural (model-choice) uncertainty. Both are stored as int16 with scale_factor 0.01 °C (precision 0.01 °C), zlib-compressed, chunked one MODIS tile per chunk. ArcticSAT1km_grid.nc holds the static 2-D lat, lon, the MOD44W land_mask and tile_index; ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc holds the monthly climatologies, the warm (April–October) and cold (November–March) seasonal means, the number of valid years per pixel and the mean inter-model spread. Note on coverage: a fixed subset of land cells never has a valid MODIS/Terra night-time LST retrieval. The pattern is static — identical in every month and year of a given tile — and varies strongly between tiles (measured examples, as a fraction of the tile's land cells: h22v02 0 %, h24v02 12.3 %, h19v02 43.4 %). There the missing night-LST predictor enters the models as zero, so the prediction rests on the remaining predictors and is less well constrained. Nothing is blanked and no quality-flag variable is provided; every file carries this note in its comment global attribute, and README_data.md lists it under "Known limitations". The climatologies in ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc use the period 2001–2025 (25 years), the earliest period in which all twelve calendar months are complete, since January and February begin in 2001. MANIFEST_md5.txt allows md5sum -c verification, MANIFEST_sizes.tsv lists file sizes, PROVENANCE.json gives a machine-readable provenance record, and README_data.md documents every variable, the method and the known limitations. Processing code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23490034 (https://github.com/SeoyeonLee-rosee/arctic-1km-sat).

title: Data and code for comparing the cooling of urban water bodies and green spaces across the aridity gradient of 229 Chinese cities
description: This record contains the data and the code of the main calculations of a study that compares the daytime and nighttime land surface temperature (LST) of urban water bodies, green spaces and built-up land in 229 Chinese cities on a 1 km grid (June–August, 2018–2023). Contents: data/cells_1km.csv.gz: 746,554 cells of 1 km with LST by day and night, water occurrence, vegetation and built-up shares, elevation, background air and dewpoint temperature, NDVI, evapotranspiration and residents; data/cities.csv: the 229 cities with their aridity index and zone and summer climate; data/results/: city-level and station-level results underlying the figures and tables of the paper; code/: Python code of the main calculations (cooling intensity, the adjusted advantage of Eq. 1, the cover effects of Eq. 2 and the water demand), with a README that lists the variables, sources and steps. Source datasets: Global Urban Boundaries, MODIS Aqua LST (MYD11A2, MYD11A1), ESA WorldCover v200, JRC Global Surface Water, SRTM, ERA5-Land, TerraClimate, MODIS NDVI (MOD13A2), ET (MOD16A2GF) and albedo (MCD43A3), PML-V2.2a, Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2, WorldPop 2020, gridded GDP per capita (Kummu et al., 2025) and the Integrated Surface Database. Only derived values are included; the source data are available from their providers. Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information 2026.

title: Bitemporal Sentinel-1/2, forest-loss and forest-carbon cells for 16 disaster and clearing sites in Indonesia
description: One row per 500 m forest cell inside an 80 × 80 km box around each of 16 Indonesian sites: 11 natural disasters (peat fires, a pyroclastic flow, eruptions, a tsunami, landslides, a cyclone, floods) and five human-clearing reference sites, 268,217 cells in total. Each cell has Sentinel-2 optical indices and Sentinel-1 radar backscatter before and after the event, the Hansen Global Forest Change loss label of the event years, terrain, ESA CCI above-ground biomass, and the carbon stock and carbon lost. Also included: independent event footprints (MODIS burned area, a Sentinel-1 flood signal, hazard-zone rules), out-of-fold and leave-one-site-out model predictions, attribution and benchmark results, supplementary tables S1–S6, Hansen loss time series 2001–2024, daily weather, hazard records, a data dictionary, and a notebook that reproduces every number of the related article (204 checks). Dataset_Description_NusaCarbon.pdf (3 pages) explains every folder and column and links every source. All inputs are public: ESA / EU Copernicus (Sentinel-1/2, Copernicus DEM, CCI Biomass), University of Maryland and Google (Hansen GFC v1.12), NASA (MODIS MCD64A1, POWER), ECMWF (ERA5), NOAA NCEI and USGS. See README.md for the folders, definitions and source terms. How to use: unzip Indonesia_disaster_forest_cells_v1.zip, read README.md, and join any files on case_id, row, col. To reproduce the article, run pip install -r code/requirements.txt, open code/reproduce_paper_results.ipynb and Run All. Related article: R. Hans et al., "Mechanism-Stratified Detection and Quantification of Disaster-Induced Forest Carbon Loss in Indonesia Using Bitemporal Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 Multispectral Observations", 2026.

title: SIAS: Stem Internal Architecture Spectrum: grass stem-architecture trait data and analysis code
description: Trait data, analysis code and result tables for the hollow-versus-solid stem-architecture dimension of the grasses (Poaceae; Cyperaceae as a solid-stemmed outgroup). DATA: 12,208 Poales species (11,602 Poaceae + 606 Cyperaceae) with stem hollowness and woodiness states compiled from Kew GrassBase, Flora of China (iPlant) and the official Flora of North America Poaceae treatment (2,054 species with documented stem state, 1,448 of them grasses); species- and genus-level environment (GBIF coordinates, WorldClim 2.1, SoilGrids, with CHELSA V2.1 and TerraClimate cross-checks, Last-Glacial-Maximum anomalies and the Global Aridity Index v3); an 11,287-tip Open Tree phylogeny with fossil-calibrated time-tree derivatives; and the result tables behind every manuscript number. Entry points: run_all_analyses.sh / reproduce_analyses.sh (R 4.5: phytools, phylolm, MCMCglmm, caper, ape; Python 3.13, see requirements.txt; HiSSE fits included as RDS). NOT REDISTRIBUTED: raw floristic texts, rasters, GBIF downloads, source trees and RNA-seq reads (licensing and size). License: CC BY-NC 4.0 (data and code).

title: EUSFlux: Mapping Forest Carbon Uptake in the Eastern US from Upscaled Flux Tower Data
description: This repository provides annual maps of Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) for eastern US forests at 500 m resolution, 2003–2023. NEP is predicted by a Random Forest model trained on AmeriFlux and NEON eddy covariance observations and applied to gridded MODIS, solar-induced fluorescence (GOSIF), Daymet and ERA5-Land predictors. Predictions are made for 16-day periods, gap-filled, and summed (day-weighted) to annual NEP. From 51 candidate predictors (Table 2 of the paper), permutation importance across 100 repetitions of 5-fold spatial cross-validation retained 13; daylength was added, giving 14: forest type, NDVI, EVI, LSWI, the 30-day LSWI anomaly, NIRv, MOD09A1 surface reflectance Bands 2, 4 and 7, LAI, SIF, root-zone soil temperature, shortwave radiation and daylength. The Random Forest (100 trees, max_features = 0.33) was tuned by nested spatial cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret it. The Zenodo repository includes: The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests; • An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimates at seven held-out flux tower test sites (test_sites_monthly_fluxComNEE_2003_2021.csv; column NEE_gC_m2_d1); • The study area boundary shapefile (StudyArea.shp); • Python scripts, Slurm job scripts and one Jupyter notebook implementing the full workflow, in four folders: input data download and checks, predictor selection and model tuning, NEP prediction and annual forest maps, and the analyses and figures of the paper (run on Indiana University’s Big Red 200 cluster; file paths must be adapted); • Annual NEP GeoTIFFs (NEP_annual_YYYY.tif, 2003–2023) at 500 m resolution. NEP is reported in units of gC m⁻² year⁻¹ in annual rasters, with positive values indicating net carbon uptake and negative values indicating net carbon release. Pixels outside each year’s NLCD forest mask are NoData. The sign convention follows NEP = −NEE; flux tower data and intermediate prediction rasters are in NEE convention and are sign-flipped in the analysis scripts. A README provided within the deposit describes the contents, formats, column names, units, and provenance of all shared data files and code. Predictor variables and benchmark data are derived from the following external datasets, which are not included in this deposit and must be obtained separately: MODIS MOD09A1, MOD13A1, MOD15A2H, MCD12Q1 and land surface temperature products (NASA LP DAAC); GOSIF SIF (University of New Hampshire); Daymet v4 (ORNL DAAC); ERA5-Land (ECMWF / Copernicus Climate Change Service); AmeriFlux/NEON flux tower observations; FLUXCOM RS+METEO (Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry); NLCD land cover (USGS), 2003–2023; forest carbon removals from Harris et al. (2021) (Global Forest Watch); and a forest stand age raster for 2010.

title: Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics: Global mangrove stand age in 2023
description: This dataset provides global mangrove stand age in 2023 at a spatial resolution of 30 m, derived from the annual mangrove extent maps of the Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics (CGMD) dataset. Stand age is defined as the number of consecutive years of mangrove presence, counted backwards from 2023 to the first year of the most recent uninterrupted period detected by CGMD. Mangroves continuously present throughout 1984–2023 are assigned to the ≥40-year age class, as their establishment may predate the satellite record. The attribute fields include age — Mangrove stand age in years. A value of 40 represents stands aged ≥40 years. Area_ha — Mangrove patch area in hectares, calculated using the World Behrmann equal-area projection. Region — Geographic region in which the mangrove patch is located. The dataset is currently under embargo and will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the associated manuscript. Please contact us if you require access before its public release.

title: Mangrove canopy height measurements from GEDI spaceborne LiDAR in 2023 and 2024
description: This dataset provides mangrove canopy height measurements acquired by the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) in 2023 and 2024. Canopy height estimates from the GEDI Level 2A RH98 metric were corrected using ground elevations from DeltaDTM to reduce height underestimation and improve agreement with independent airborne LiDAR measurements. Each footprint was also assigned a mangrove stand age from our global mangrove age map for 2023. The attribute fields include Attribute — GEDI shot number identifying each footprint. year — Year of the GEDI observation. rh98 — Original RH98 canopy height estimate from the GEDI Level 2A product, in metres. rh98_Corre — Corrected canopy height estimate using DeltaDTM ground elevations, in metres. age — Mangrove stand age in 2023, derived from our age map and expressed in years. Stands continuously present throughout 1984–2023 are classified as ≥40 years old. The dataset is currently under embargo and will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the associated manuscript. Please contact us if you require access before its public release.

title: Bolivia Fire benchmark data and reproduction artifacts
description: Bolivia Fire version 0.1.0 provides a weekly VIIRS S-NPP standard-processing satellite-detection benchmark for Bolivia and its retained reproduction evidence. The strict panel contains 37,146 cells, 678 Monday issues from 2013-01-07 through 2025-12-29 and 25,184,988 cell-weeks. The target is a selected satellite detection, not a count of fires, ignitions or burned area, and is not an official warning. Three independently extractable ZIP64 archives use repository-relative paths: benchmark-data: panel, cells, CHIRPS rainfall, MOD13A2 vegetation, MapBiomas Collection 4 land-cover and combined features, schemas and manifests. reproduction-artifacts: configurations, environment lockfile, fitted models and calibrators, retained predictions and alternative-learner cached vectors, evaluation history, figure JSON, family-specific producing revisions and historical source registries. raw-inputs: FIRMS CSV snapshots, MOD13A2 AppEEARS subset, CHIRPS native windows, MapBiomas aggregate exports, boundaries, GeoNames and outage HTML. Top-level README, licence notices, data dictionary, member inventory and SHA-256 checksums describe the files. Dataset reuse is supported. Recalculation from saved predictions is partially supported: strict primary validation/test exports and alternative-learner cached vectors are retained; rainfall, sensitivity and vegetation, land-cover and combined covariate per-row prediction exports and standalone scored-row masks are absent. Their result records and fitted models remain available. Recomputing any final-test metric is a logged test opening under the frozen protocol; release verification does not open the test. Rebuilding from raw inputs is partially supported. Global CHIRPS rasters, MODIS HDF granules and native MapBiomas 30 m maps are not supplied; MapBiomas re-extraction requires an Earth Engine account. Operational live forecasts, serving derivatives, regenerable caches, temporary files and logs are excluded. Later environmental experiments are separate from the original CHIRPS comparison; retained 2026 availability evidence does not establish a completed confirmation evaluation. Known discrepancies include an older unmatched cell-place manifest hash, fourteen unretained intermediate states, the MOD13A2 acquisition AOI buffer of 0.05 degrees versus the registered 0.1 degrees, and CatBoost GPU digit-level nondeterminism. See the record README for details and producing-code revisions. Load serialized model files only from trusted sources. Compiled and derived data are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Upstream raw inputs retain NASA open-data/public-domain or attribution terms detailed in LICENSES.md, including CHIRPS, MapBiomas and GeoNames CC BY 4.0 and GeoBolivia public-domain boundaries. Code is separately MIT licensed at Cupesi/bolivia-fire. Cite the dataset version and the software separately.

title: Pre- and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and elevation differences for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli/Rasuwa catastrophic flood
description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal and Tibet. We provide here pre-event and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from Pléiades, SPOT6 and SPOT5 stereo-images. Date were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES. The collection includes three files: Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_pre-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_post-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_dh.tif =========================== Methods The post-event DEM is purely based on Pleiades stereo images. The pre-event DEM is based mostly Pléiades and SPOT6 stereopairs. A small fraction of the pre-event DEM was derived from 10 m SPOT5-HRS images. All DEMs were generated at a ground sampling distance of 4 m using the semiglobal matching algorithm of the Ames Stereo Pipeline (Beyer et al., 2018; Shean et al., 2016) and the processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). A ground sampling distance of 10 m was used for SPOT5-HRS. All individual DEMs were first co-registered and vertically adjusted to the Copernicus 30 (GLO-30) DEM, masking out glaciers using the Randolph Glacier Inventory v7 (RGI 7.0 consortium, 2023). Next, the individual pre- and post-event DEMs were co-registered in pairs to construct the most accurate DoD possible. Finally, those individual DoDs were mosaicked in a single map of elevation difference. The uncertainty on the mean elevation change was calculated using the patch method (Dussaillant et al., 2018). This approach aims to empirically determine the uncertainty associated with the mean elevation change by sampling patches (or tiles) of stable terrain of various sizes to constrain the decay of error with increasing averaging area (Miles et al., 2018; Wagnon et al., 2021). The stable terrain was defined here as excluding glaciers and a buffer around the river channels where erosion or deposition has occurred. For a 1 km² averaging area, the 1-sigma (68th percentile) error and the 2-sigma (95th percentile) error were calculated to be ±0.8 and ±1.8 m, respectively. Beyer, R. A., Alexandrov, O., and McMichael, S.: The Ames Stereo Pipeline: NASA's Open Source Software for Deriving and Processing Terrain Data, Earth and Space Science, 5, 537–548, https://doi.org/10.1029/2018EA000409, 2018. Deschamps-Berger, C., Gascoin, S., Berthier, E., Deems, J., Gutmann, E., Dehecq, A., Shean, D., and Dumont, M.: Snow depth mapping from stereo satellite imagery in mountainous terrain: evaluation using airborne laser-scanning data, The Cryosphere, 14, 2925–2940, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-14-2925-2020, 2020. Dussaillant, I., Berthier, E., and Brun, F.: Geodetic Mass Balance of the Northern Patagonian Icefield from 2000 to 2012 Using Two Independent Methods, Front. Earth Sci., 6, 8, https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2018.00008, 2018. Miles, E. S., Watson, C. S., Brun, F., Berthier, E., Esteves, M., Quincey, D. J., Miles, K. E., Hubbard, B., and Wagnon, P.: Glacial and geomorphic effects of a supraglacial lake drainage and outburst event, Everest region, Nepal Himalaya, The Cryosphere, 12, 3891–3905, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-12-3891-2018, 2018. Nuth, C. and Kääb, A.: Co-registration and bias corrections of satellite elevation data sets for quantifying glacier thickness change, The Cryosphere, 5, 271–290, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-5-271-2011, 2011. RGI 7.0 Consortium: Randolph Glacier Inventory - A Dataset of Global Glacier Outlines, Version 7.0., 2023. Shean, D. E., Alexandrov, O., Moratto, Z. M., Smith, B. E., Joughin, I. R., Porter, C., and Morin, P.: An automated, open-source pipeline for mass production of digital elevation models (DEMs) from very-high-resolution commercial stereo satellite imagery, ISPRS J. Photogramm., 116, 101–117, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2016.03.012, 2016. Wagnon, P., Brun, F., Khadka, A., Berthier, E., Shrestha, D., Vincent, C., Arnaud, Y., Six, D., Dehecq, A., Ménégoz, M., and Jomelli, V.: Reanalysing the 2007–19 glaciological mass-balance series of Mera Glacier, Nepal, Central Himalaya, using geodetic mass balance, Journal of Glaciology, 67, 117–125, https://doi.org/10.1017/jog.2020.88, 2021. =========================== Data Specifications: Cartographic projection: UTM zone 45N (EPSG:32645) Origin of Elevation: meters above WGS84 ellipsoid Raster data format: GeoTIFF NoData value : -9999 This dataset includes only DEMs because a licence needs to be signed with CNES to access Pléiades imagery. =========================== Acknowledgements: Pléiades post-event images were obtained using the CIEST² service developed with CNES by FormaTerre, the solid Earth component of the Data Terra research infrastructure (https://www.poleterresolide.fr/ciest-2-nouvelle-generation-2/). Pléiades and SPOT6 pre-event stereo images were provided through Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and the Pléiades World Heritage (Pléiades © CNES 2019, distribution AIRBUS DS) SPOT5 images were obtained through the Spot World Heritage (https://regards.cnes.fr/user/swh/) =========================== Dataset Attribution: This dataset is licensed under a Creative Commons CC BY-NC 4.0 International License (Attribution-NonCommercial). =========================== Citation: Please cite this repository as described below: Etienne Berthier. title: Simulated OCO-2 data, split tables, trained model weights, and predictive artifacts for amortized probabilistic CO2 retrieval
description: Simulated OCO-2 soundings and everything needed to reproduce the amortized probabilistic retrieval described in the accompanying paper. Version 3 adds the operational a priori of every reference sounding in February, March and July 2020 (oco2_apriori.tar.gz): the a priori state vector and its covariance, and the a priori XCO2 and its pressure-weighting function. These are the prior baselines added to the paper in its second revision. Every other archive is unchanged from version 2. Version 2 adds, to the February 2020 delivery already in version 1: the reference-disjoint, within-reference, all-February and training-size split tables, each with the standardization constants estimated from its own training partition (oco2_splits.tar.gz); the trained checkpoints of all six models on each of the three splits reported in the paper (oco2_model_weights_v2.tar.gz); the two held-out months, March and July 2020, as the archives the scoring jobs consumed — spectra, ACOS profile covariances, covariates and the month split table (oco2_month_202003_full.tar.gz, oco2_month_202007_full.tar.gz); and the per-sounding predictive artifacts from which every table and figure in the paper is regenerated without a GPU (oco2_scoring_artifacts.tar.gz). Version 1's archives are included unchanged. oco2_model_weights.tar.gz is the original submission's checkpoints, kept for provenance and superseded by the _v2 archive. The paper's numbers come from the reference-disjoint split table group_split_v1_cov.csv and the _v2 weights. CONTENTS.md describes each archive and SHA256SUMS.txt covers all of them. The code that reads them is at https://github.com/acallesalda/oco2-amortized-uq, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22667577; scripts/get_data.sh downloads, verifies and unpacks everything to the paths the code expects. The simulation experiment, its a priori and the operational ACOS L2FP retrievals were produced at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology.

title: Knowledge graph and dataset of global storms (1990–2023)
description: Storms of the eleven storm subtypes recorded in the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT) from 1990 to 2023, in 3,492 storm-country records, with the hazard, exposure, vulnerability and cascade context that can shape their impacts. For each record with administrative units from Geo-Disasters, hazard and exposure measures suited to its subtype were read over the storm's units and days in Google Earth Engine: ERA5 and ERA5-Land, the Gridded Population of the World v4, the Global Human Settlement Layer, SRTM, ESA WorldCover, the low elevation coastal zone grid v3, MERRA-2, CHIRPS and Global Mangrove Watch. Storm surge comes from the Global Tide and Surge Model v3, and best tracks from IBTrACS, with wind fields modelled in CLIMADA. Displacement records of the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) and appeals of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) are matched to storms. Vulnerability comes from UNDP's Human Development Index and the World Bank's World Development Indicators and Worldwide Governance Indicators. Cascades link storms to disasters that struck the same area within 91 days. Every value has a status column and, when empty, a gap column that gives the reason, and every link states its method and confidence. Files: - Tables of comma-separated values, one per class of the graph, linked by the keys in schema.yaml - storms_public.ttl.gz: the Resource Description Framework knowledge graph (Turtle), linked to Wikidata, with its vocabulary, SHACL shapes and VoID description - data_dictionary.csv: every column, its unit and its meaning - query1.rq–query6.rq: the competency questions in SPARQL Storms of the eleven storm subtypes recorded in the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT) from 1990 to 2023, in 3,492 storm-country records, with the hazard, exposure, vulnerability and cascade context that can shape their impacts. EM-DAT's values are not redistributed, as its licence forbids it. Records are keyed by EM-DAT's disaster number, and users can obtain the values from CRED at https://public.emdat.be. The processing code rebuilds the full dataset, with the SQLite database and the complete graph, from a user's own export.

title: Riparian agroforestry insetting in the climate refugia of the Paraná–Paraguay Basin: data and code
description: This dataset provides the result tables and the analysis code underlying the article "From phantom to functional: riparian agroforestry insetting for fruit-eating migratory fish" (submitted to Academia Environmental Sciences and Sustainability). The study starts from the climate refugia identified for two fruit-eating migratory fishes of the Parana-Paraguay Basin, Piaractus mesopotamicus and Myloplus tiete, in do Couto et al. (2026), Academia Biology 4(2), doi 10.20935/AcadBiol8362. Within the 1935 refugia cells of 10 km that require riparian restoration, it maps the riparian vegetation deficit in 100 m buffers, estimates the potential carbon dioxide sequestration, compares the 20-year net present value of passive regeneration, assisted regeneration and agroforestry with yerba mate and native fruit trees, and ranks micro-basins into investment tiers with a composite insetting index. The dataset contains three parts. 1. Refugia cells (GeoPackage, EPSG:6933). The 1935 cells of 10 km x 10 km that require riparian restoration, with the attributes inherited from the previous study. 2. Tables (CSV and JSON). Riparian vegetation deficit per micro-basin and landscape composition per cell; current and reference above-ground biomass, soil organic carbon and potential carbon dioxide sequestration of the 450,512 riparian pixels of 1 ha, with centroid coordinates; for the 171,192 restorable pixels with carbon gain, the climatic suitability of yerba mate, the land opportunity cost, the net present value of the three scenarios, the internal rate of return and the payback period; the 10,000 Monte Carlo draws and the Sobol indices of the economic assumptions; the five sub-indices and the composite insetting index per pixel; and the index, carbon, net present value and investment tier of the 2462 micro-basins. A pixel identifier links all pixel tables, and micro-basins are identified by the HydroBASINS level 10 code. 3. Code. The Python and Google Earth Engine scripts of the five phases of the analysis, of the successive re-runs and of the figures, including the final economic analysis (spatial land cost, suitability-scaled revenue, Monte Carlo simulation and Sobol decomposition) and the script that audits the consistency of the results. Monetary values are given in Brazilian reais and in United States dollars, converted at R$5.4443 per USD (mean PTAX selling rate of the Central Bank of Brazil from 16 October 2024 to 15 October 2026). title: 16 October 2022 Pléiades (CNES) pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Rasuwa catastrophic flood
description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Rasuwa region in Nepal and Tibet : https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/ We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades stereo acquired on the 16 October 2022, 4 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The collection includes two DEM: 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_20m_aligned.tif 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total DEMs in 2x2m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean’s dem_align implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). 2022-10-16_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the 2 m and 20 m described above DEMs retaining the highest resolution where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. Beyer, R. A., Alexandrov, O., and McMichael, S.: The Ames Stereo Pipeline: NASA's Open Source Software for Deriving and Processing Terrain Data, Earth and Space Science, 5, 537–548, https://doi.org/10.1029/2018EA000409, 2018. Deschamps-Berger, C., Gascoin, S., Berthier, E., Deems, J., Gutmann, E., Dehecq, A., Shean, D., and Dumont, M.: Snow depth mapping from stereo satellite imagery in mountainous terrain: evaluation using airborne laser-scanning data, The Cryosphere, 14, 2925–2940, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-14-2925-2020, 2020. Nuth, C. and Kääb, A.: Co-registration and bias corrections of satellite elevation data sets for quantifying glacier thickness change, The Cryosphere, 5, 271–290, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-5-271-2011, 2011. =========================== Data Specifications: Cartographic projection: UTM zone 45N (EPSG:32645) Origin of Elevation: meters above WGS84 ellipsoid Raster data format: GeoTIFF NoData value : -9999 This dataset includes only DEMs because a licence needs to be signed with CNES to access Pléiades imagery. =========================== Acknowledgements: Pléiades images were provided by Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and the Pléiades World Heritage (Pléiades © CNES 2019, distribution AIRBUS DS) =========================== Dataset Attribution: This dataset is licensed under a Creative Commons CC BY-NC 4.0 International License (Attribution-NonCommercial). =========================== Citation: Please cite this repository as described below: Etienne Berthier. title: Global-scale streamflow simulation framework used in the paper of "Abrupt surface water decline during 2023–2024 record warming"
description: Summary: This repository contains the data and source code for a global-scale streamflow simulation framework utilizing an ensemble of machine learning models. The methodology addresses the challenge of hydrological variability by implementing a climate-zone-specific training approach. Results from the Step 3 script can be extrapolated globally to simulate monthly streamflow across all HydroSHEDS basins in the subsequent step. Key technical features: Specialized ensembles: The framework employs five machine learning architectures: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, SVM, Neural Networks, and Gaussian Process Regression. Climate segmentation: Basins are categorized using an Aridity Index (AI) threshold of 0.65. Asymmetric weighting: To mitigate common overestimation issues in arid hydrology, dry-region models are trained with a 2x penalty for overestimation errors. Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA): Individual model outputs are integrated using climate-zone-specific BMA weights to produce a robust final simulation. Dataset contents: Input data: Compiled monthly training features, observed monthly streamflow for 150 basins (lat/long for each gauge provided), optimized hyperparameters, and geospatial shapefiles. Output data: Fully trained model objects, calibrated annual time series, and performance evaluation visualizations. Source code: A comprehensive MATLAB script for data imputation, model training, and metric calculation (see step3_ML_DL_fulltraining_inputs_outputs_rep3_PWeighted_optim.m). Temporal Coverage: 1991 – 2025.

title: Ranked ephemeral wetland candidates for South Carolina, USA, derived from lidar, Sentinel-1 SAR, and soil survey data
description: Introduction Ephemerally-flooded wetlands, characterized by seasonal flooding and drying cycles, play crucial roles in water regulation, biogeochemical cycling, and biodiversity conservation. However, despite their ecological significance, ephemeral wetlands face threats from anthropogenic disturbances, a rapidly changing atmospheric equilibrium, and weakened regulatory protections. Recognizing the importance of these ecosystems is crucial for their conservation and sustainable management. There is currently no statewide map of ephemeral wetlands across all geographic zones. To address this gap, we developed a Wetland Atlas for South Carolina, focusing on the major river basins focusing on ephemeral wetlands. This digital atlas will provide a comprehensive inventory of identified wetland locations, allowing stakeholders to prioritize areas for protection and restoration efforts. By adopting a landscape approach and leveraging existing protected lands, we aim to enhance conservation strategies and promote spatial connectivity among ephemeral wetlands across the state. The National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) was established in 1974 and led by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service “to inventory wetland area, location, type, and trends — the foundational information needed to better manage wetlands and their many benefits” (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2025, para. 3). The NWI provides spatial boundaries and attribute information describing wetlands ranging from small, ephemeral features (<1 ha) to large, complex riverine and estuarine systems spanning thousands of hectares. The original NWI maps were delineated by hand using aerial imagery, soils data, and other available information. Collectively, these data provide one of the most comprehensive spatial inventories of wetlands in the United States and support applications at continental, state, county, and local scales. NWI data are used for wetland management and conservation as well as recreational applications, including birding, hunting, fishing, and boating (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2025). The accuracy of the NWI is known to be an issue for wetlands due to “the age of the data, include a relatively large (0.5 ac.) minimum mapping size, relatively coarse resolution of the source imagery, and inclusion of many features that do not meet the current common definition of ‘wetland’” (Gale, 2021, p. 1). Gale (2021) led a North Carolina statewide effort where 103,000 acres of field surveys were used to assess the NWI. The surveys included 4,655 individual wetlands with sizes ranging from <0.01 to 1,271 ac. and found that “>90% of field verified wetlands were below the NWI minimum mapping size of 0.5 ac.” (Gale, 2021, p. 1). Overall, these results suggest that the NWI underestimates approximately 60,000 ac. of wetlands in the state (Gale, 2021). South Carolina shares a similar climate and ecoregions as North Carolina including the Blue Ridge, Piedmont, Southeastern Plains, Mid-Atlantic Coastal Plain, and also includes the Southeastern Coastal Plain that is not present in North Carolina. We make the assumption that given these similarities between SC and NC that there are similar issues with the NWI in SC. One of the classification issues with ephemeral wetlands is that these tend to be small and are seasonally inundated depressions that the National Wetlands Inventory has systematically under-mapped because they are too small for the imagery NWI was compiled from, dry for much of the year, and often under forest canopy. This project asks a narrow question of closed depressions (sinks) across the state within existing protected areas mapped under the USGS PAD-US: Do they resemble the wetlands NWI did map based on soil, terrain, land cover, and radar backscatter? The output is a ranked list of unmapped sinks that have similar characteristics to existing NWI wetlands across all SC counties and ecoregions. Specifically, we use a positive-unlabeled (PU) approach with a gradient boosting machine learning (ML) algorithm. The PU approach was used because we know where existing NWI boundaries are, including their attributes and classification schemes, but we do not know where other wetlands exist, based on the assumption that small ephemeral wetlands were likely underrepresented during the NWI mapping efforts. To support the identification of these unknown wetlands, we generated a sink layer for every county in SC. For this research, we identified sinks or topographic depressions derived from USGS DEMs that are characterized by interior drainage (Lindsay, 2023), using primarily 1-m lidar-derived DEMs, but in some instances we had to fall back to older 3-m DEMs due to the lack of updated coverage for some counties. These hydrological depressions do not have surface outflows and thus represent areas that have the potential to retain or pond water, but this does not mean they are wetlands. Lane et al. (2018) provide a detailed discussion of the water storage capacity of depressional non-floodplain wetlands. It is acknowledged that the identification of sinks does not indicate a wetland, but we use the sinks as landscape characteristics to build a ranking system of potential wetlands that closely match NWI-characterized wetlands. Thus, our work generates a ranking rather than a probability. Scope and interpretation This report summarizes the clustered positive-unlabeled sink model. Counties are grouped into clusters based on measured predictor behavior, and one model is fitted per cluster, so scores are comparable within a cluster and are not comparable between clusters. Positive prevalence of labeled NWI wetlands in the training data differs substantially from cluster to cluster due to physiographic differences across the landscape. Coastal and near-coastal counties tend to have relatively flat landscapes and thousands of sinks, as compared to the western Piedmont/Blue Ridge counties, which are characterized by more prominent elevation changes, well-defined drainage, and fewer input sinks and NWI wetlands available to serve as positive labeled sinks. Additionally, the NWI itself contains errors in both directions: some areas mapped as wetland are not actually wetlands, and some real wetlands exist but were not mapped. This omission error is skewed by size, as smaller wetlands are more difficult to delineate given the methods and complexities of wetland identification. This impacts the analysis because a binary labeling approach is used: positive NWI-labeled sinks are used to estimate the probability that an unlabeled sink more closely matches the labeled NWI sinks within each cluster. Elkan and Noto (2008) identify this issue and propose methodologies to address it: “Under the assumption that the labeled examples are selected randomly from the positive examples, we show that a classifier trained on positive and unlabeled examples predicts probabilities that differ by only a constant factor from the true conditional probabilities of being positive” (p. 1). A classifier that scores unlabeled sinks by their similarity to the positive sinks is expected to produce lower values than a classifier trained against the true population would. In other words, the output probabilities reported here are lower than they would be if we were working with a known true population of NWI wetlands to train the model on unlabeled sinks. Elkan and Noto (2008) do discuss methods to calculate a corrected classifier value, but we do not attempt that in this work. The model produces a single probability score per unlabeled sink, and sinks are ranked within each cluster on a scale from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates no similarity to the NWI positive set and 1 indicates a 100% probability of matching the NWI positive labeled data set. Thus, each unlabeled sink is tagged with a score that essentially functions as a ranking from 0 to 1 within each cluster. We present those findings and model performance in this work. An additional output not presented here is the final GIS layer, in which every unlabeled sink in every county is identified with its score. Those data will be available on ArcGIS.com. A high-scoring sink is a candidate for field verification, not a wetland determination or delineation.

title: County-Level US Corn Yield Lead-Time Forecasting Benchmark (Corn Belt, 2000–2025)
description: This dataset is a county-year modeling matrix for benchmarking in-season corn yield forecasts across the US Corn Belt, assembled entirely from public data products. It supports reproducible lead-time forecasting, feature-ablation, uncertainty, historical-baseline, feature-cap sensitivity, and tabular and temporal model-comparison experiments for the study How Early Can a Corn Yield Forecast Be Trusted? The matrix contains 22,797 county-year records and 594 columns spanning 2000–2025 across 12 Corn Belt states (IL, IN, IA, KS, MI, MN, MO, NE, ND, OH, SD, and WI). Counties are identified by 5-digit FIPS codes. The prediction target is raw USDA NASS county corn grain yield (yield_bu_acre, bushels per acre). Features are derived from public sources and include monthly and weekly GRIDMET weather; heat-stress indicators (GDD, KDD, and EDD); GRIDMET drought indices (SPEI, SPI, and PDSI); MODIS vegetation and land-surface indices (NDVI, EVI, NDWI, GCI, LAI, FPAR, and LST); multi-depth POLARIS and OpenLandMap soil properties; LGRIP30 irrigation fraction; US Census and SRTM geographic covariates; USDA NASS crop progress and condition reports; and lagged historical yield features. MODIS vegetation, LAI/FPAR, and LST features use a prior-year (Y−1) USDA CDL corn mask, preventing same-year land-cover information from entering the features. Full per-column documentation is provided in benchmark_matrix_dictionary.csv; upstream product and asset IDs, native resolutions, and aggregation methods are provided in source_provenance.csv. This release matches the associated paper’s final analysis scope: 22,797 county-years from 1,009 reporting counties over 2000–2025. The reproduction loader reads the matrix directly, with no additional row filtering required. Files include benchmark_matrix.parquet (primary), benchmark_matrix.csv (plain-CSV fallback), benchmark_matrix_dictionary.csv, benchmark_matrix_build_report.csv, source_provenance.csv, README_DATA.md, LICENSE, and MANIFEST.txt with SHA-256 checksums. Important: yield_trend and yield_anomaly are full-record descriptive columns and must not be used as forecast inputs. The reproduction code constructs the valid past-only historical trend for each training and prediction setting. Released under CC BY 4.0. Please cite both this dataset and the associated paper.

title: JRC Global Proxy Maps of Managed and Unmanaged Forest
description: The dataset provides maps of Managed and Unmanaged Forests at a global scale, with spatial resolutions of 5 km and 50 km. These maps serve as a proxy for countries' managed and non-managed forest areas, produced to support comparability between independent estimates and national Greenhouse Gas (GHG) reporting under the UNFCCC. The methodology uses country maps of managed forests where available, but also makes assumptions where official data is not present, employing independent datasets that may not be fully consistent with national forest definitions when no other options are available. Here, we present the version 2.0 (2026) of the “Global JRC Proxy Maps of Managed and Non-Managed Forests,” which is used to “translate” DGVMs (Dynamic Global Vegetation Models) results into national inventory definitions in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (Friedlingstein et al., 2026). Country-level results of this translation are available through the Global Land Use Carbon Fluxes Data Hub: https://forest-observatory.ec.europa.eu/carbon/fluxes. Compared to version v.1, in this version v.2 the managed forest definitions of several countries were updated according to the information provided within their Biennuial Transparency Reports (BTRs). This dataset will be updated as better information becomes available.

title: GLEAM4-HR: Daily 1 km Land Evaporation and Soil Moisture over the Meteosat Disk (2018–2022)
description: 1. Dataset Overview This dataset contains daily estimates of terrestrial evaporation (E), its individual components, evaporative stress, and surface and root-zone soil moisture from GLEAM4-HR, a high-resolution implementation of the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM4). GLEAM4-HR provides spatially continuous estimates at approximately 1 km resolution (0.00833°) over the Meteosat disk for the period 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2022. The dataset covers Europe, Africa, and parts of South America and the Middle East, extending from 81°W to 61°E and from 41°S to 81°N. GLEAM4-HR combines process-based E modelling with machine-learning estimates of evaporative stress, an irrigation scheme informed by irrigation and crop-phenology information, and the assimilation of Sentinel-1 soil moisture observations (Baez-Villanueva et al., 2026). The complete archive comprises approximately 2.03 TB of daily NetCDF files, organised into seven variable-specific directories. 2. Data Access The complete GLEAM4-HR dataset is distributed through Globus, a platform for reliable, high-performance transfer of large scientific datasets. Access to GLEAM4-HR: GLEAM4-HR Globus Collection GLEAM website: www.gleam.eu Interactive visualisation: gleam.lexcube.org Users can retrieve individual daily NetCDF files, complete variable directories, or the entire dataset. 2.1 Downloading data directly to a personal computer Users can download GLEAM4-HR to their personal computers using Globus Connect Personal, available for Windows, macOS, and Linux. To transfer data locally please follow these steps: Access Globus: Visit https://www.globus.org and sign in using an institutional account or another supported identity (GitHub, ORCID, or Google account). Select your computer as the destination: In the Globus File Manager, select your personal Globus collection in the destination panel and navigate to the desired local directory. Start the transfer: Click Start to initiate the transfer. Progress can be monitored through the Globus Activity page. title: Reference test set and example code for: Six decades of satellite observations reveal the footprint of ion-adsorption rare earth mining in Ganzhou in southern China largely absent from global maps
description: This record contains the reference test set and example code supporting the estimates of the manuscript "Six decades of satellite observations reveal the footprint of ion-adsorption rare earth mining in Ganzhou in southern China largely absent from global maps". The test set is an independent stratified sample of 775 Landsat pixels across Ganzhou, Jiangxi Province, China, drawn systematically from a random start within each stratum. For each pixel it gives the stratum, the map class, the values of the compared products (three global mining inventories, the official mining areas, Global Forest Change, GLC_FCS30D and leachate tank locations) and the reference labels interpreted from declassified photographs of 1964–1970, the Landsat record and dated very high resolution images, without pixel coordinates. The record also holds the sizes of the 23 strata, an example subset of 30 mapped patches with their annual series, and Python example code that recomputes the area, accuracy and capture estimates of the manuscript. A separate table gives the results of a single-date experiment, in which 89 known rare earth locations of an earlier reference sample were interpreted on the 2 m Gaofen mosaic of 2025 alone. Version 1.1 corrects version 1.0. In version 1.0, the column single_date_2m_result of data/test_set.csv attached the results of the first single-date experiment to test pixels with the same identifiers, but the experiment interpreted locations of an earlier reference sample. The column has been removed, and the results are given in data/single_date_experiment1.csv. The sampling design is now described as stratified systematic sampling from a random start within each stratum. All other data are unchanged. The mapped patches and the reference data are original results of our research group and are reserved for further work. The complete patch dataset and the pixel coordinates are available from the authors for collaborative research; please contact the corresponding author, Yuandong Wang (wangyuandong@gnnu.edu.cn). title: Greenhouse gas concentrations in high-Arctic streams in northeast Greenland and their relationships with stream chemistry and catchment characteristics
description: Description: Dataset on greenhouse gas concentrations and driver variables in headwater streams in the Zackenberg area, Northeast Greenland measured during three field campaigns 2021-2023. Methods are described below. Field sampling methods The 18 study streams are located in the Northeast Greenland National Park, near the Zackenberg Research Station (74°28’N, 20°34’W). The area has a polar tundra climate with mean annual air temperature of -9.1 °C; July is the warmest month with a mean of 5.8 °C, and February the coldest month with a mean of -22.4 °C and continuous permafrost. Annual mean precipitation is 261 mm of which approximately 10% falls as rain (Hansen et al., 2008). The 18 catchments spanned a gradient from steep, sparsely vegetated slopes with shallow, coarse mineral soils and limited snow retention, to low-gradient, wetter catchments with peat accumulation and more continuous vegetation cover. At each site (50-70 m reach), we measured stream discharge using the salt tracer release method (Gordon et al. 2004), and specific conductivity with a Cond 3110 WTW portable meter. We measured stream width at 10 points, and water depth at 50 points along the reach. We filtered water samples in the field: for dissolved nutrient analyses, we used 0.2 µm membrane filters (Supor 200 PES, Pall Corporation, Port Washington, New York, US), and for DOC/TDN analyses we used 0.7 µm pre-combusted glass fibre filters (GFF, Whatman, UK). Samples for nutrients were kept frozen until analysis, while samples for total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) and DOC were acidified with HCl 10% to pH 2-3 and stored refrigerated at 5 °C. We also measured pH in the field. All water samples and measurements were made in the middle of the streams’ width and depth. We estimated dissolved CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations in stream water using the headspace equilibration technique (McAuliffe, 1971). In the field, we collected replicate (n=3) 50 mL water samples from the upper 10 cm of the water column using a 60 mL polypropylene syringe. We then introduced 10 mL of N2 gas into each syringe to create a headspace and shook each syringe vigorously for ∼60s. Finally, the 10 mL headspace was transferred into a 5.9 mL pre-evacuated borosilicate glass vial (Exetainer, Labco, High Wycombe, UK) until analysis. Sample analysis We analyzed nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) using standard methods on a Lachat QC-8500 Flow Injection Autoanalyzer (colorimetric analysis; Lachat Instruments, Loveland, Colorado, US; APHA, 2005), and quantification limit for NO3-N and NH4+-N were 4 and 10 µg N L-1, respectively. Samples for TDN and DOC were analyzed on a TOC-Vcph/TNM-1 analyzer (chemiluminescence analysis; Shimadzu) with QL of 0.055 mg N L-1. The QL for DOC was 0.02 mg C L-1. Dissolved organic N (DON) was calculated by subtracting DIN (NO3--N + NH4+-N) from TDN. All data below the QL were expressed as half of the QL (QL/2). In the laboratory, we measured CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations using a dual-inlet Agilent 7890 GC system interfaced with a CTC CombiPal autosampler (Agilent, Nærum, Denmark), configured and calibrated using standard gases as described in detail by Petersen et al. (2012). We converted headspace gas concentrations to dissolved aqueous concentrations according to Henry's law, using Henry's constant to correct for water temperature and atmospheric pressure at the time of sampling (Weiss 1974; Weiss and Price 1980; Wiesenburg and Guinasso 1979). For each gas and sampling event, we calculated the % saturation as %sat = 100 × Cw/Ceq, where Cw is the measured dissolved gas concentration and Ceq is the concentration in equilibrium with the atmosphere, calculated from Henry’s law as Ceq = KH(T) × pgas. Here, KH(T) is the solubility coefficient at the in-situ water temperature (Weiss 1974; Weiss and Price 1980; Wiesenburg and Guinasso 1979), and pgas is the atmospheric partial pressure of the gas, calculated from atmospheric mixing ratios of 415 ppm for CO2, 1.80 ppm for CH4, and 0.330 ppm for N2O and the atmospheric pressure at the time of sampling. Thus, water temperature was used both to calculate the dissolved gas concentrations and their equilibrium concentrations Catchment characteristics Terrestrial vegetation density across the study area was quantified using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) derived from Sentinel-2 imagery. Images were obtained from the ESA Copernicus Open Access Hub, selected for lack of cloud cover, with a spatial resolution of 12 m. The temporal window for NDVI data was specifically delineated to early July, August, and September 2021, and early August 2023, to coincide with the field measurements of GHGs. The data were corrected for atmospheric bottom effects, with acquisition dates stamped as follows: 9Jul2021, 1Aug2021, 4Sept2021, and 2Aug2023. All NDVI values were computed from the Red (B4) and Near-Infrared (B8) bands using the formula (NIR−R)/(NIR+R) within a raster calculator, subsequently producing GeoTIFFs of the NDVI. For each catchment area, NDVI distribution was examined, and the median NDVI was calculated using the zonal statistics tool in ArcGIS pro. In addition, for each stream catchment, snow cover was also derived from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. Scene classification maps were downloaded from the ESA Copernicus Open Access Hub for the same days and regions as the NDVI imagery. The classification map was then overlaid with the catchments using the zonal statistics tool to estimate the snow cover for each catchment. The scene classification maps have a spatial resolution of 20 m, i.e. coarser than the NDVI data, but fine enough to resolve snow patches within the study catchments (0.24–11.3 km2). Finally, the catchment area, mean elevation, and terrain slope were derived using ArcticDEM, a high-resolution global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for territories north of 60° latitude, sourced from the Polar Geospatial Centre at the University of Minnesota (USA). For this study, processed mosaics with a 2 m spatial resolution were used and subsequently down-sampled to a 7 m spatial resolution using average resampling to reduce imagenoise. Arctic DEM was employed in ArcGIS Pro with spatial analyst tools to precisely delineate and model characteristics of the small-scale headwater stream catchments. References Gordon, N. D., McMahon, T. title: Development drivers, CO2 emissions and ecological footprint in developing economies, 2000 to 2025: research database and R code
description: A documented panel of the 163 economies that the World Bank classified as low or middle income in at least one fiscal year from FY2001 to FY2025, with the R script that runs the whole analysis. The panel covers 2000 to 2025: 4,238 country-years and 119 columns. It is the research database of the doctoral dissertation "AI-Enhanced Modeling of Development–Environment Interactions in Developing Economies: Integrating Econometric and Explainable Machine Learning Approaches" (Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences, MATE, 2026) and of the journal manuscripts drawn from it. The panel holds two outcomes, CO2 emissions per capita and the ecological footprint of production per capita, and eight explanatory variables: population growth, GDP per capita growth, trade openness, urbanization, the renewable share of final energy, industry value added, energy intensity and mean years of schooling. It also holds alternative and extra series, sample flags and two break dummies. Every value of the ten core variables has a status (published, second source, estimate, nowcast or national source). 83 values come from national statistical sources under written rules, each with its publishing body, table and link. 46 gaps in the explanatory variables are filled by multiple imputation in 50 datasets. The R script reads the data file and produces every result table, from the checks of the database to the last robustness check: panel models, Random Forest, XGBoost, SHAP values and the checks on the 50 imputed datasets. A full run takes about 12 hours on a laptop. One series is left out of the data file. The 3,900 values of CO2 per capita that are computed from the IEA-EDGAR CO2 file of EDGAR 2026 are empty, because that file is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and its licence does not allow a database built from it to be shared. The file itself is included unchanged under its own licence, and the script computes the values again from it. The 250 values from the Global Carbon Budget are included, and so is the Global Carbon Budget series (column co2_pc_gcb). The column biomass_cooking (WHO Global Health Observatory) is empty because of the WHO terms of use. No result uses it. README.md says how to run the script. title: Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code
description: # Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code ## Overview This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce the analysis of structural deficits in the conceptual rainfall-runoff model SIMHYD. The method works as follows: - A differentiable version of SIMHYD carries correction slots of identical structure and capacity on eight fluxes (S1–S8). - Forcing errors and observation errors are modeled separately from structural errors. - A deficit is localized by comparing competing single-slot hypotheses with a significance test. The comparison uses streamflow and, where available, soil moisture, evapotranspiration (ET) and snow water equivalent (SWE). - After localization, only the localized slots are repaired, and the repair is evaluated with variables not used in training. The package covers two applications: 1. **Synthetic experiments.** Ten types of implanted structural deficits (D1–D9) and compound deficits (C1–C3) are tested, together with a no-deficit control (D0). Two independently generated truth sets are used (realizations r0 and r1), with eight observation combinations, two observation-quality levels and three types of input error. 2. **Application to 156 CAMELS basins** in the conterminous United States. Training uses streamflow, ESA CCI soil moisture, ERA5-Land or GLEAM evaporation, and UA SWE. Independent evaluation uses FLUXCOM-X-BASE ET and MODIS NDVI. All results shown in the figures and tables of the associated article can be recomputed from the files in `data/results/`. The 12 figure scripts in `code/figs/` reproduce the article figures pixel for pixel from this package. ## Package structure ``` structural-deficit-localization/ ├── README.md this file ├── LICENSE licenses of the code and the data ├── code/ Python code (see code/README.md) │ ├── README.md │ ├── LICENSE MIT License │ ├── requirements.txt │ ├── paths.py locations of the data folders │ ├── models/ differentiable SIMHYD, truth models, correction slots │ ├── data/ readers for CAMELS, Daymet and the gridded observation products │ ├── synth/ generator of the synthetic truth and observations │ ├── train/ losses and the localization model / trainer │ ├── scripts/ experiment runners │ ├── eval/ analyses that produce the summary tables │ ├── figs/ figure scripts │ └── tests/ unit tests └── data/ input data and experiment outputs (see data/README.md) ├── README.md ├── LICENSE CC BY 4.0, with the conditions for third-party data ├── basins/ list of the 156 basins with their groups ├── camels/ CAMELS attributes, basin boundaries, basin forcing, Daymet forcing ├── basin_observations/ basin means of the gridded observation products ├── model_input/ synthetic and real data sets read by the experiments └── results/ outputs of all experiments and summary tables ``` ## Quick start All commands are run from the `code/` folder. The code was tested with Python 3.9 on Windows 10; the package versions are listed in `code/requirements.txt`. ``` cd code pip install -r requirements.txt python -m unittest discover -s tests -t . # 37 tests, about 3 minutes on a CPU python -m figs.fig2_synthetic_success # writes figures/fig2_synthetic_success.png/.pdf ``` The figure scripts `figs.fig1_schematic` to `figs.fig9_ndvi` and `figs.figS1_precip_prior` to `figs.figS3_phenology_maps` read only `data/` and write to a new `figures/` folder at the package root. The map figures use cartopy, which downloads the Natural Earth 1:50m boundaries on first use. To rerun the experiments themselves, see `code/README.md`. The full set of experiments takes several days on a desktop computer with a 16-core CPU and one 12 GB GPU; a single experiment tag takes between about one hour and one day. A GPU is optional. ## Source data The basin-level data in `data/` were derived from the following public data sets. Users of these data should follow the terms of use of the original providers. | Data set | Use in this package | Provider and link | |---|---|---| | CAMELS-US time series and attributes | streamflow, forcing (P, T, PET), basin attributes, basin boundaries, Daymet basin forcing | NCAR, https://doi.org/10.5065/D6MW2F4D and https://doi.org/10.5065/D6G73C3Q | | ESA CCI Soil Moisture v09.2 COMBINED | soil moisture observations | CEDA, https://doi.org/10.5285/d4e66299f5054129b8076fb7502949e1 | | ERA5-Land | total evaporation and potential evaporation | Copernicus Climate Data Store, https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.e2161bac | | GLEAM v4.3a | actual and potential evaporation | https://www.gleam.eu | | UA SWE (NSIDC-0719) | snow water equivalent | NSIDC, https://doi.org/10.5067/0GGPB220EX6A | | FLUXCOM-X-BASE | ET for independent evaluation | ICOS Carbon Portal, https://doi.org/10.18160/5NZG-JMJE | | FLUXCOM RS ensemble | ET, additional comparison only | https://www.fluxcom.org | | MOD13C1 v006 NDVI | independent evaluation of the phenology formulation | NASA LP DAAC, https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD13C1.006 | The raw gridded products are not included. The scripts in `code/data/` that compute the basin means from the raw files are included; see `code/README.md`. ## License The code in `code/` is released under the MIT License (`code/LICENSE`). The data produced in this work are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (`data/LICENSE`). These are the synthetic data sets, the experiment outputs and summaries, and the basin list. The basin-level data derived from the third-party products listed above remain subject to the terms of use of their original providers. ## Contact Jun Guo, prof_guojun@hust.edu.cn

title: Towards a more complete quantification of the global carbon cycle
description: These are the data and IDL code required to create Table3 from the paper. Abstract. The main components of global carbon budget calculations are the emissions from burning fossil fuels, cement production, and net land-use change, partly balanced by ocean CO2 uptake and CO2 increase in the atmosphere. The difference between these terms is referred to as the residual sink, assumed to correspond to increasing carbon storage in the terrestrial biosphere through physiological plant responses to changing conditions (ΔBphys). It is often used to constrain carbon exchange in global earth-system models. More broadly, it guides expectations of autonomous changes in global carbon stocks in response to climatic changes, including increasing CO2, that may add to, or subtract from, anthropogenic CO2 emissions. However, a budget with only these terms omits some important additional fluxes that are important to correctly infer ΔBphys. They are cement carbonation and fluxes into increasing pools of plastic, bitumen, harvested-wood products, and landfill deposition after disposal of these products, and carbon fluxes to the oceans via wind erosion and non-CO2 fluxes of the intermediate break-down products of methane and other volatile organic compounds. While the global budget includes river transport of dissolved inorganic carbon, it omits river transport of dissolved and particulate organic carbon, and the deposition of carbon in inland water bodies. Each one of these terms is relatively small, but together they can constitute important additional fluxes that would significantly reduce the size of the inferred ΔBphys. We estimate here that inclusion of these fluxes would reduce ΔBphys from the currently reported 3.6 GtC yr–1 down to about 2.1 GtC yr–1 (excluding losses from land-use change). The implicit reduction in the size of ΔBphys has important implications for the inferred magnitude of current-day biospheric net carbon uptake and the consequent potential of future biospheric feedbacks to amplify or negate net anthropogenic CO2 emissions.

title: The Global Long-term Microwave Vegetation Optical Depth Climate Archive VODCA
description: Related paper containing detailed description: Moesinger et al. (2020) Vegetation optical depth (VOD) describes the attenuation of radiation by plants. VOD a function of frequency as well as vegetation water content, and by extension biomass. VOD has many possible applications in studies of the biosphere, such as biomass monitoring, drought monitoring, phenology analyzes or fire risk management. We merged VOD observations from various spaceborne sensors (SSM/I, TMI, AMSR-E, AMSR2, WindSat) to create global long-term vod time series. Prior to aggregation the data has been rescaled to AMSR-E, removing systematic differences between them. There is a product for C-band (~6.9 GHz, 2002 - 2018), X-band (10.7 GHz, 1997 - 2018) and Ku-band (~19 GHz, 1987 - 2017). The data is global sampled on a regular 0.25 degrees grid. Each product is available as daily global netcdf4 files. Currently there is an issue with opening the file using ESA SNAP. As an alternative Panoply can be used to quickly visualize the data. An update of VODCA, addressing this issue and potentially including an extension of the dataset, is foreseen to be published on Zenodo early 2020. Please contact us if you have any questions, problems or suggestions for improvement! title: Global database of river width, slope, catchment area, meander wavelength, sinuosity, and discharge
description: 1.Summary This document describes the database that accompanies the article written by the authors of this dataset and accepted by Geophysical Research Letters (doi: 10.1029/2019GL082027).The database is distributed as a set of shapefiles, containing polylines that define the geometry of river centerlines located between 60°N and 56°S, with attributes described below. The shapefiles are organized according to continent and further broken into major basins to allow for manageable file sizes. A more complete dataset is available in the netCDF format upon request (please email Renato Frasson at renato.prata.de.moraes.frasson@jpl.nasa.gov). This database was partially funded by the Algorithm Definition Team contract to the Ohio State University, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and Remote Sensing Solutions, Inc. 2.Polyline geometry The centerline geometry is defined by sets of points located approximately every 30 m based on the Global River Widths from Landsat (GRLW) database (Allen & Pavelsky, 2015; 2018). Each line describes a meander and features the following attributes. 3.Attribute description SegmentID: identification number of the river segment (segments are parts of a river delimited by confluences). lakeFlag: 0 – river, 1 – lake, 2 – river under the influence of tide, 3 – canal, 4 – unable to connect GRWL with HydroSHEDs, 5 – dam, -9999 – no data. Width: average width in the meander, disregarding small river widths assigned to locations undetected by Landsat but known to be inundated. Locations where no width could be produced are marked as -9999. Elevation: mean elevation from SRTM (90m) per river meander in meters. SRTM pixels are assigned to equally spaced points (every ~30m) over the river centerlines using the nearest neighbor approach. The average elevation of all valid points per meander is reported here. Locations where no elevation could be produced are marked as -9999. Slope: water surface slope in centimeter per kilometer. Slope is initially computed over 10 km reaches, then used to compute optimum reach lengths using a modified version of the equation proposed by LeFavour and Alsdorf (2005) in the form of RL=2σ /S, where RL is the optimum reach length, σ is the height uncertainty (5.51 m from LeFavour and Alsdorf, 2005) and S the initial slope estimate. Final slopes are computed over the optimum reach lengths using elevations assigned to the 30 m river points using either classic linear regression or the Theil-Sen estimator depending on which method produces the best coefficient of determination. Locations where no slope could be produced are marked as -9999. Meandwave: Meander wavelength in meters. This is computed by first smoothing the 30 m resolution river centerlines using a 5-point moving average and then identifying inflection points on the smoothed river centerlines. Finally, the meander wavelength takes the value of twice the distance between consecutive inflection points according to the definition given by Leopold and Wolman (1960). Sinuosity: Dimensionless sinuosity of each river meander computed the ratio of the length between meander endpoints measured along the river centerline to half the meander wavelength as defined by Leopold and Wolman (1960). catch_area: Catchment area was derived from flow direction and corresponding flow accumulation grids based on HydroSHEDS (Lehner et al., 2008). The flow accumulation grid describes, for any location (i.e. pixel), the number of upstream raster pixels that drain to that particular location. We translated flow accumulation given in number of pixels into catchment area (in m2) by multiplying the number of pixels flowing to a location by the average area of SRTM pixels according to the latitude of the centroid of the river segment. QWBM: mean annual flow estimated with the water balance model WBMsed (Cohen et al., 2014). Strpwr_len: stream power normalized by width (W/m). Strpwr_are: stream power normalized by area (W/m2). Acknowledgements Use of this database should be acknowledged appropriately. The WBM data used in this database were provided by Dr. Albert Kettner at INSTAAR, University of Colorado at Boulder.
